A clique of heads lowers the ternary dense threshold from \(N^{3/2}\) to \(N\log N\) for clique-covering blocks

21 September 2026 · Working extension of the ternary graph criterion · Narrows the window for clique-covering blocks to a factor of about \(10^{12}\Lambda\); structured blocks unaffected. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question. The next step after the route review is the intermediate-rank endpoint for \(p=3\). The ternary graph criterion excludes blocks whose projected rank is at most \(R\) or at least \(Q_*=\Theta(N^{3/2}\sqrt{\log N})\). The missing implication is the window between. This cycle tests whether the dense threshold is an artifact of the image bound rather than of the kernel method, using the dyadic random inventory and the recorded structured controls as calibration. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The chance that this narrows the window was judged moderate at the outset, because the method's actual requirement is a degree-\(k\) Macaulay quotient, which the recorded proof bounds only through its degree-two leading monomials.

Where the dense threshold comes from

The recorded kernel condition (DH-membership) asks only that \(f=\sum_ic_ig_i+E\) with \(\deg c_i\le k-2\) and \(E\in I_k(\Gamma_H)\), that is, \(f\) lies in the degree-\(k\) Macaulay span of the block's inputs plus old relations. Each block's cost is the codimension of that span in the degree-\(k\) squarefree space. The proof bounds it by the number of independent sets of size at most \(k\) in the head graph of degree-two leading monomials, (DH-count), which is at most \(4\binom sk\exp(k^2/s-qk/s^2)\) for \(q\) distinct heads. Under lexicographic order, the degree-two initial set of a generic tuple of rank \(q\) is the \(q\) largest pairs \(x_1x_2,\ldots,x_1x_s,x_2x_3,\ldots\): about \(t=q/s\) centers, each adjacent to every vertex. This is a split graph whose centers form a clique of size about \(q/s\), and its independent sets are counted by the clique bound below with \(m\approx q/s\), giving the factor \(e^{-qk/s^2}\). A weight order can instead make the heads a clique on about \(\sqrt{2q}\) vertices. The gain comes from the size of the clique, so for generic tuples the recorded bound loses because of the order, not because of the blocks.

Lemma: a clique of heads acts like an affine core

Let \(s\ge2\), \(1\le k\le s/4\), \(1\le m\le s/4\), and let a graph on \(s\) vertices contain a clique on a set \(M\) of \(m\) vertices. Then the number of its independent sets of size at most \(k\) satisfies \[ J_{\le k}\ \le\ 8\binom sk\exp\!\left(-\frac{mk}{2s}\right). \tag{CH-count} \] Proof. An independent set contains at most one vertex of \(M\), so the number of independent \(j\)-sets is at most \(\binom{s-m}{j}+m\binom{s-m}{j-1}\). Since \(m+k\le s/2\), \(m\binom{s-m}{k-1}\le\frac{2mk}{s}\binom{s-m}{k}\), and \(\binom{s-m}{k}\le\binom sk(1-m/s)^k\le\binom sk e^{-mk/s}\). For \(j<k\) the terms decrease at least by the factor \(\frac{j+1}{s-m-j}\le\frac12\) as \(j\) decreases, so the sum over \(j\le k\) is at most twice the \(j=k\) term. Hence \(J_{\le k}\le2(1+2x)e^{-x}\binom sk\) with \(x=mk/s\), and \((1+2x)e^{-x/2}\le4\) for \(x\ge0\).

Realizing the clique as heads. Multilinearize with Booleanity first, so no squares remain. Order monomials by degree, then by the weight \(w_M\) that gives each coordinate of \(M\) weight one and every other coordinate weight zero, then lexicographically. This is a monomial order. Suppose every pair inside \(M\) is the leading monomial, under this order, of some element of the span of the block's inputs plus the old degree-two relations, that is, \[ \binom M2\subseteq\operatorname{in}_{w_M}\bigl(\operatorname{span}(g_i)+I_2(\Gamma_H)\bigr)_2 . \tag{CH-hyp} \] Then full reduced row echelon form on all \(\binom m2\) columns of pairs inside \(M\) supplies, for each such pair \(e\), a combination of inputs plus an old certificate whose leading monomial is \(e\) and whose other quadratic terms all have lower weight; without full reduction, other pairs of \(M\) have equal weight and are only lexicographically smaller. Old \(I_2\) elements used as reducers are absorbed in the old residual \(E\). The recorded monomial-by-monomial reduction applies unchanged, and its image dimension is at most (CH-count). This refines the distinct-head count; the nearest recorded head-choice device, for cyclic local domains, uses disjoint pairs only. A block whose quadratic coefficient space, reduced as in the recorded dense case, projects onto all coordinates of \(\binom M2\) satisfies (CH-hyp).

Theorem: clique blocks join the ternary criterion

Keep every hypothesis and parameter of the ternary graph criterion: \(\mathbb F_3\), the separated graph with \(s=15(N+1)\) coordinates, \(M_{\rm blk}\) complete accuracy-one old-quadratic blocks, \(\Lambda=\log(64(M_{\rm blk}+1))\), \(k=\lceil\sqrt{N\Lambda}\rceil\), and \(TD+k\le N/10^6\). Put \[ m_*=\left\lceil\frac{2s}{k}\left(\frac{5k^2}{N}+\Lambda+\log2\right)\right\rceil=O(\sqrt{N\log N}), \] and assume \(m_*\le s/4\). Allow a third kind of block: one satisfying (CH-hyp) for some coordinate set \(M\) of size \(m_*\), with its own weight order. Then the source still has no ordinary PC refutation through \(D\).

Proof. For such a block, (CH-count) gives image dimension at most \(8e^{-m_*k/(2s)}\binom sk\le\binom sk e^{-5k^2/N}/(16(M_{\rm blk}+1))\), which is the per-block share the recorded proof allots to dense blocks. The kernel element \(f\) then satisfies (DH-membership) for this block with \(\deg c_i\le k-2\) and an old \(I_k(\Gamma_H)\) residual, exactly as for a dense block. The recorded weight maps and original-degree certificates, \(\beta_i=fc_i\) and \(fg_iP(\beta)=g_i(f-f^3)+f^2g_iE\) within \(3k+2\), apply verbatim. The sum of all image dimensions stays below \(\dim W_k\), so a common nonzero \(f\in W_k\) exists, and the recorded replay derives it over the old graph base through \(TD+k\), contradicting separation.

Rank needed. After subtracting the pairs of \(M\) already covered by quadratic parts of old \(I_2(\Gamma_H)\), (CH-hyp) forces projected block rank at least \(\binom{m_*}2\approx1.6\times10^4\,N\Lambda\) minus that number, compared with \(Q_*=\Theta(N^{3/2}\sqrt\Lambda)\) for the dense case. The low-rank case reaches \(R\approx N/(4.4\times10^7)\): at the ceiling \(D=4p-1=11\) of the complete-board compiler (the criterion itself only requires \(D\ge5\)), \(T=2H_*+4R+2\) and \(TD+k\le N/10^6\) allow \(R\) linear in \(N\), not only \(N^\sigma\). For blocks satisfying (CH-hyp) whenever their rank permits, the open window therefore shrinks from \([N/(4.4\times10^7),\ \Theta(N^{3/2}\sqrt{\log N})]\) to \([N/(4.4\times10^7),\ 1.6\times10^4N\Lambda]\), a factor of about \(7\times10^{11}\Lambda\).

Calibration

Dyadic random inventory. For a uniformly random linear form \(F=\sum a_ux_u\) over \(\mathbb F_3\), the quadratic part of \(1-F^2\) modulo Booleanity has coefficient \(-2a_ua_v=a_ua_v\) on \(x_ux_v\), the off-diagonal part of \(aa^{\mathsf T}\). The projections of \(h\) independent such forms onto \(\mathbb F_3^{\binom M2}\) fail to span exactly when some nonzero zero-diagonal symmetric \(B\) has \(a^{\mathsf T}Ba=0\) for all \(h\) samples. In odd characteristic \(a\mapsto a^{\mathsf T}Ba\) is a quadratic form of rank \(r=\operatorname{rank}B\ge2\), whose zero proportion is \(1/3+O(3^{-r/2})\) by the standard count of zeros of quadratic forms over finite fields, and at most \(5/9\) for every \(r\ge2\). Stratify the union bound by rank. There are at most \(3^{rm}\) such \(B\) of rank \(r\), so ranks \(r<4\log_3m+c\) contribute at most \(3^{(4\log_3m+c)m}(5/9)^h\). The remaining at most \(3^{\binom m2}\) matrices contribute at most \(3^{\binom m2}3^{-h}e^{O(1)}\), because then \(3h\cdot3^{-r/2}=O(1)\) once \(h=O(m^2)\). Hence \(h\ge\binom m2+c'(\log m+\Lambda)\) makes the failure probability at most \(e^{-\Lambda}\) for fixed \(M\), for suitable absolute constants. This uses the recorded fact, from the two-size control, that graph restriction and row projection leave the coefficients uniform. Dyadic blocks with \(h_L=\lceil100L\ln L\rceil\) above \(\binom{m_*}2+c'(\log m_*+\Lambda)\) are therefore excluded, as are those below \(R\). The blocks left are those with \(h_L\) in \([N/(4.4\times10^7),\ 1.6\times10^4N\Lambda]\): about \(\log_2(7\times10^{11}\Lambda)\approx39+\log_2\Lambda\) dyadic scales. The inventory still defeats the extended criterion, but only through that band.

Structured controls. The recorded common-factor control has every quadratic term through one coordinate, so no pair inside a set avoiding that coordinate is a head and (CH-hyp) fails for every \(M\) of size at least two; it remains a one-probe case. The reserve-coordinate triple family has disjoint heads, so (CH-hyp) fails, consistent with the exact-image barrier, whose true image is too large for any reduction; that family is sparse and belongs to the support endpoint. The lemma does not claim a dichotomy for blocks that satisfy neither (CH-hyp) nor the recorded cases.

Assessment and next step

The kernel method's dense threshold was mostly an artifact of the lexicographic head graph. A weight order concentrating heads on a clique lowers it to \(\Theta(N\log N)\) for blocks whose span covers a clique of pairs, which includes random dense blocks of sufficient rank by the stratified bound above. The remaining window for such blocks is a factor of about \(7\times10^{11}\Lambda\). Closing it needs either a better separator, to lower both constants, or a sharper Macaulay-quotient bound using higher-degree consequences rather than degree-two heads. For structured blocks, a separate probe or support dichotomy is still needed.

Next step. Test whether the constant-factor band can be closed for random dense blocks with a Macaulay-quotient bound beyond degree-two heads, which for generic tuples predicts codimension about \(e^{-qk^2/s^2}\binom sk\) rather than \(e^{-\sqrt q\,k/s}\binom sk\). A table of semi-regular regularity-degree predictions, the first nonpositive coefficient of \((1+t)^s(1+t^2)^{-h}\), is retained with its script; it is heuristic orientation, not evidence for any bound. Separately, formulate the dichotomy for blocks failing (CH-hyp): a large projected clique, or a small coordinate set whose conditioning removes most of the quadratic rank.

Verification gate. Re-read the recorded distinct-head lemma, the ternary criterion and its proof; claim searches for clique and weight-order head choices found only a disjoint-pair device. A fresh-context reviewer, briefed narrowly, confirmed (CH-count), the monomial order, \(m_*\), the low-rank reach and the verbatim transfer of the dense-block proof. It required six corrections, all adopted: the lexicographic head graph is a split graph with a clique of about \(q/s\) centers, not a star forest; multilinearization and full reduced echelon form before taking heads; subtraction of pairs covered by old \(I_2\) in the rank requirement, and the explicit window constant; a link for \(D=11\); a proof, rather than an assertion, of the random projection threshold; and the refinement link. No computation beyond the prediction table was run.

The contracting-homotopy proposal reduces to sequential elimination; savings need the common-weight kernel method

21 September 2026 · Negative test of a proposed mechanism; dual reformulation of recorded results · The explicit construction reproduces additive elimination exactly; savings require polynomial selectors under a shared weight. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question and tests. In conversation the proposal was to start from Razborov's reduction operator for PHP, a contracting homotopy onto the old algebra, and add blocks with the homological perturbation lemma, hoping that the series \(\sum(\delta h)^n\) terminates at a cost independent of the number of blocks. The user assigned two tests: (1) the one-block series must reproduce one-block elimination at cost \((p-1)\delta=(p-1)^2\) for selector inputs; (2) on the historical two-block conflict (Example 6.5), the series must cost less than repairing moments. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The closed moment tower had already shown that the functional-side object reduces to the mixed-moment system, so the chance of a new mechanism was judged low at the outset; the test decides whether the series construction avoids that reduction.

NS: the perturbation series has one term

For Nullstellensatz, take the two-term complex whose degree-one part is formal products of monomials and axioms, with differential multiplication, and whose degree-zero part is \(\mathcal P_{\le D}\) in the joint ring of old and fresh variables, the old complex being extended to that ring. A contraction consists of a projection \(R\) onto a complement of \(I_D\) and a certificate chooser \(h\) with \(1-R=dh\) in degree zero. Adding a block adds new degree-one generators, companions times monomials, with differential \(\delta\) landing in degree zero. Since \(h\) maps into degree one and \(\delta\) is defined only on the new generators, \(\delta h=0\), so the transferred differential is just \(R\delta\). The perturbed quotient is \(\operatorname{im}R\) modulo \(R\) applied to the companion multiples. This is the prescribed-moment system again: the lemma adds no information in NS. For PC, Razborov's operator is not a chain contraction but a projection with \(R(xt)=R(xR(t))\) below the ceiling, and we know of no perturbation lemma for that fixed-point condition. The construction therefore has to be read off the one-block proof.

Test 1: the explicit dual of one-block elimination

Let \(\mathcal G\) be the old system with field equations, and add one block with inputs \(g_j\) of degree at most \(\delta\). Put \(D'=D+(p-1)\delta\). For an input \(g_j\) and \(\alpha\ne0\), let \(\sigma_{j,\alpha}\) set \(r_{1,j}=\alpha^{-1}\) and every other fresh variable to zero, and let \(\sigma_0\) set all fresh variables to zero. The proof of Theorem 7.6 shows that \[ \chi_\alpha(g_j)\,\sigma_{j,\alpha}\bigl(C_D(\mathcal G+\text{block})\bigr)\subseteq C_{D'}(\mathcal G). \] Every augmented axiom maps into old consequences within \(D'\), and historical Lemma 1.4 carries the inference steps. Assume \(1\notin C_{D'}(\mathcal G)\), so normalized old annihilators exist. Dually, the following dichotomy holds.

  • If for some \(j\), some \(\alpha\ne0\) and some normalized old annihilator \(\Lambda\) of \(C_{D'}(\mathcal G)\) has \(\Lambda(\chi_\alpha(g_j))\ne0\), then \(F\mapsto\Lambda(\chi_\alpha(g_j)\sigma_{j,\alpha}(F))/\Lambda(\chi_\alpha(g_j))\) is a normalized annihilator of \(C_D(\mathcal G+\text{block})\). The block fires with a constant selector on the input value \(g_j=\alpha\), weighted by \(\chi_\alpha(g_j)\) of degree \((p-1)\delta\).
  • Otherwise every normalized old annihilator kills \(\chi_\alpha(g_j)\) for all \(j\) and all \(\alpha\ne0\). Normalized annihilators span all annihilators, so every such \(\chi_\alpha(g_j)\) lies in \(C_{D'}(\mathcal G)\), and by the exact identity \(g=\sum_{\alpha\ne0}\alpha\chi_\alpha(g)\) of historical (eq:selectorlinear), of degree \((p-1)\delta\le D'\), so does every \(g_j\). Reusing these lines as in the proof gives \(\sigma_0(C_D(\mathcal G+\text{block}))\subseteq C_{D'}(\mathcal G)\). So \(\Lambda\circ\sigma_0\) works for any old annihilator \(\Lambda\) of \(C_{D'}(\mathcal G)\): no weight is needed, but the old functional is still required through \(D'\).

For selector inputs \(q=1-L^{p-1}\), \(\delta=p-1\) and the cost is \((p-1)^2\), as Test 1 required. The dual construction is explicit, but it is a case split with a weight, not a perturbation series.

Several blocks: every block costs the same

Iterating the dichotomy in reverse level order, as in historical Theorem 7.7, lowers the working degree by \((p-1)\delta_a\) for every block, whether it fires or not: in both bullets the old functional must annihilate \(C_{D'}\), because the second bullet only places the inputs in \(C_{D'}\), not in \(C_D\). A block is free only if its inputs already lie in \(C_D\) at the current working degree. So the explicit construction reproduces the additive cost \(D+(p-1)\sum_a\delta_a\) exactly and saves nothing. For inputs in old variables, the resulting functional is \(\Lambda_{\rm old}\) applied to \(F\) specialized and multiplied by the weights of the fired blocks; for blocks above level one each weight is itself specialized by the substitutions of the lower levels. Reading these products as the terms of \(\sum(\delta h)^n\) is only an analogy, since the NS computation above gives \(\delta h=0\).

Savings in this construction would require a block to be certified at the current degree without a weight, or several blocks to share one weight. Historical Lemma 7.9 shares a constant-substitution weight among blocks with equal input span. The common-weight kernel method of the ternary graph criterion and its clique extension goes beyond this construction: it uses polynomial selectors \(\beta_i=fc_i\) under one weight \(f\) lying in every block's degree-\(k\) Macaulay kernel, and a common \(f\) exists when the kernels' codimensions sum below the separated space. So the kernel method extends the dichotomy from constant to polynomial selectors, and it is the only recorded mechanism of this kind that shares one weight across blocks with different input spans.

Test 2: the two-block conflict

In Example 6.5 both blocks have the constant input \(1\), so \(1\) lies in every input span and Lemma 7.9 eliminates them at zero degree cost; the weighted construction fires both with constant selectors and no weight. The conflict in that example arises between single-block moment corrections chosen independently, which the sequential construction never makes. The example therefore does not discriminate. A discriminating case needs many fired blocks with different input spans, and there the only recorded way to share weights is the kernel counting.

Assessment

Test 1 passes: the explicit dual of one-block elimination costs \((p-1)^2\) per selector block. Test 2 is passed trivially, because the example is not a discriminating case. Made explicit, the contracting-homotopy proposal is sequential elimination and costs \((p-1)\delta\) for every block. Within constant substitutions it gains only for equal spans; beyond them, the recorded route to inventory-independent cost is the polynomial-selector kernel method, now extended by the clique-head endpoint. Together with the closed moment tower and the route review, the topological proposals tested today all reduce to recorded mechanisms. The open question they point to is the same: a common weight for many firing blocks with different input spans in the intermediate-rank window.

Next step. For odd-prime-clause-transfer, return to the intermediate window: a degree-\(k\) Macaulay-quotient bound beyond degree-two heads for random dense blocks, and a clique-or-probe dichotomy for structured blocks. The local-to-global cohomology lead should be reopened only with a concrete presheaf and a vanishing mechanism for sharing weights.

Verification gate. Re-read historical Theorems 7.6 and 7.7, Lemma 7.9, Example 6.5, and the recorded ternary criterion with its clique extension. A fresh-context reviewer, briefed narrowly, confirmed the NS computation, the dichotomy, the exact selector identity and the Test 2 verdict. It required corrections, all adopted: a non-firing block is still certified only through \(D'\), so every block costs \((p-1)\delta\) and the drafted per-fired-block cost was wrong; lower-level substitutions act on higher-level weights; the series reading is only an analogy; the kernel method extends rather than instantiates the construction; and the dichotomy's quantifiers and standing hypothesis are now explicit. Global tools: new leads, and what sheaf gluing on the matching site can add

21 September 2026 · Working proof of two linear-algebra gluing criteria; leads recorded · The dyadic test is formulated, not decided. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question. After three topological constructions reduced to recorded mechanisms (complex review, moment tower, homotopy test), the user asked for tools that see global rather than local structure. The missing implication is unchanged: one object, a weight or design, that works for polynomially many blocks with different input spans. This cycle records the leads not yet in the notebook and then formulates the sheaf lead on the matching site precisely, testing it against the dyadic random inventory. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer.

Leads

The sheaf and cohomological-consistency lead is item 3 of the augmented-obstruction entry, with the Ó Conghaile and Chan–Ng references and the common-root control; it is not restated. This entry adds its concrete site, below. The only proved gluing tool in the record is the main notebook's tree-gluing lemma for functionals on subalgebras generated by linear spaces under a running-intersection condition. Its companion observation shows that designs for every proper subfamily of one row need not glue. Three leads are new.

  1. Excess intersection. The kernel method succeeds when the blocks' degree-\(k\) Macaulay kernels meet in a nonzero element, and it proves this only by counting codimensions, as if the kernels were in general position. Excess intersection theory (Fulton), with degeneracy-locus classes (the Porteous formula) and Schubert calculus in Grassmannians, studies intersections of special families that are larger than expected. These are statements over algebraically closed fields, so transferring them to nonzero intersections of \(\mathbb F_p\)-subspaces would need its own argument. A statement that PHP structure forces such excess for intermediate-rank blocks would close the window left by the clique-head endpoint. No candidate statement exists yet.
  2. Forcing and nonstandard models. Ajtai's lower bound for PHP in bounded-depth Frege was proved by forcing over nonstandard models, and Krajíček's forcing with random variables builds Boolean-valued models from families of random variables on sample spaces. This is the global tool with a record against PHP itself; it is closer to logic than to topology, and it bears on the main notebook's goal as well as this thread.
  3. Topoi. Topos approaches to local versus global consistency (for example Isham and Döring) and the sheaf-theoretic, cohomological treatment of contextuality by Abramsky with Brandenburger, and later Mansfield and Barbosa, largely repackage sheaf cohomology. A lower bound would still have to come from computing a specific sheaf's cohomology on a specific site, which is the sheaf lead. Lowest priority.

These are literature leads recorded at the user's request, not imported theorems about this source.

Site one: the poset of restrictions

Let \(\mathcal R\) be a set of partial matching restrictions \(\rho\), and for each \(\rho\) let \(A_\rho\) be a space of functionals on degree-\(\le D\) polynomials over the residual board. Restriction \(F\mapsto F|_\rho\) does not raise degree, so every \(\lambda\in A_\rho\) pulls back to a functional \(\lambda\circ\mathrm{res}_\rho\) on the full board.

No gluing with a bottom element. Restrictions ordered by extension have the empty restriction as least element, so a presheaf of designs on this poset has its global sections at the empty restriction. The recorded restriction method is exactly the pullback of one local section: if \(\lambda\) annihilates the residual source's closure, then \(\lambda\circ\mathrm{res}_\rho\) annihilates the source's, because a restriction maps source derivations to residual derivations. No gluing is involved, and a single restriction must handle every block. The dyadic inventory defeats exactly this.

Mixtures: an exact criterion. The new freedom is a linear combination \[ \Lambda=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}w_\rho\,\lambda_\rho\circ\mathrm{res}_\rho \] of pulled-back local functionals that need not annihilate anything individually, provided their errors cancel. Let \(S\) be the span of all such pullbacks and \(W=C_D(\text{source})\). A normalized \(\Lambda\in S\) annihilating \(W\) exists if and only if \[ 1\notin W+S^\perp,\qquad S^\perp=\{F:\ \lambda(F|_\rho)=0\ \text{for all }\rho\in\mathcal R,\ \lambda\in A_\rho\}. \tag{MX} \] Proof. \(S\cap W^\perp=(S^\perp+W)^\perp\) in finite dimension, and a subspace of functionals contains one with \(\Lambda(1)\ne0\) exactly when \(1\) lies outside its annihilator.

If each \(A_\rho\) is the full annihilator space of the residual old consequences \(C_D(\Gamma|_\rho)\), then \(S^\perp=\{F: F|_\rho\in C_D(\Gamma|_\rho)\ \forall\rho\}\supseteq C_D(\Gamma)\). When this space lies inside \(W\), for example when \(\mathcal R\) contains the empty restriction, (MX) is just \(1\notin W\) and unconstrained mixtures restate the problem. Otherwise they give a strictly stronger sufficient condition, still with no construction. A construction comes from restricting the local sections to explicitly built ones, such as the designs produced by the recorded endpoints on residual boards; then \(S^\perp\) is determined by those constructions.

Site two: covers by subspace domains

Let \(V_1,\ldots,V_t\) be subspaces of a filtered polynomial space and \(\lambda_a\) functionals on \(V_a\) that agree on every pairwise overlap \(V_a\cap V_b\). They have a common extension to \(\sum_aV_a\) for every such choice exactly when the Mayer–Vietoris sequence \[ \bigoplus_{a<b}V_a\cap V_b\longrightarrow\bigoplus_aV_a\longrightarrow\sum_aV_a\longrightarrow0 \tag{MV} \] is exact in the middle, that is, when every relation \(\sum_av_a=0\) with \(v_a\in V_a\) is a sum of overlap relations. Call the middle homology \(H_1\) of the cover. Proof. The \(\lambda_a\) define a functional on \(\bigoplus V_a\) vanishing on the image of the overlaps; it descends to \(\sum V_a\) exactly when it vanishes on the kernel of the sum map, and every compatible family does so exactly when that kernel equals the image. The recorded tree-gluing lemma, stated over \(\mathbb F_2\), gives a sufficient condition for this vanishing for covers by truncated algebras \(A(U_a)_{\le b_a}\), and it needs agreement only along tree edges rather than on all pairs; (MV) is the general criterion.

Two examples show that \(H_1\) captures known obstructions.

  • The recorded row obstruction. In the old quotient, cover one row by the algebras of its coordinates \(X_{ij}\). Pairwise overlaps are constants, yet \(\sum_jX_{ij}=1\) is a relation among the pieces that no combination of overlap relations produces. It is a nonzero class of \(H_1\), and it is the degree-one relation that the recorded observation identifies as blocking global gluing.
  • Three concurrent lines. Over \(\mathbb F_3\), cover the degree-\(\le2\) part of \(\mathbb F_3[a,b]/(a^3-a,b^3-b)\) by the algebras of \(a\), \(b\) and \(a+b\), each spanned by \(1,L,L^2\). The direct sum has dimension nine and maps onto the six-dimensional space spanned by \(1,a,b,a^2,ab,b^2\), since \((a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2\). The kernel has dimension three. Pairwise overlaps are the constants, whose relations span two dimensions. So \(H_1\) is one-dimensional, spanned by \(a+b-(a+b)=0\): local functionals agreeing on constants glue only if \(\lambda_1(a)+\lambda_2(b)=\lambda_3(a+b)\). This is the linear shadow of the three-selector configuration, in which every pair of the forms \(a,b,a+b\) behaves while the triple does not; it is an analogy, not an identification with the recorded degree-six obstruction.

The dyadic test

Subspace covers are vacuous for dense blocks. Every input of a dyadic block is a random form on the whole board, so each block's domain is the whole algebra and every cover of this kind is trivial. Site two can only help blocks with localized supports, which the support endpoints already handle.

Restriction mixtures reduce to error cancellation. Take as local sections the designs produced by the extended graph criterion on residual boards of size \(L\), ignoring the blocks whose projected rank at size \(L\) falls in the open window, a band of about \(40+\log_2\Lambda\) dyadic scales. Each such design annihilates the residual closure of the source without its band's blocks. Let \(\mathrm{band}(b)\) be the residual sizes \(L\) at which block \(b\)'s projected rank lies in the window. If that rank is roughly constant across sizes, as for the dyadic tuples while their size stays below the number of residual pairs, \(\mathrm{band}(b)\) is an interval of about \(40+\log_2\Lambda\) dyadic values; in general it depends on the projected rank at each \(L\). For the Nullstellensatz part, a mixture over sizes gives a design if, for every block \(b\), \[ \sum_{L\in\mathrm{band}(b)}\ \sum_{\rho\ \text{with residual size}\ L}w_\rho\,\lambda_\rho\bigl((mE^b_i)|_\rho\bigr)=0 \quad\text{for all legal multipliers }m\text{ and inputs }i, \] with normalization \(\sum_\rho w_\rho=1\). Blocks outside every band contribute nothing. A PC annihilator must in addition kill closure elements whose derivations pass through band blocks; (MX) with \(W=C_D(\text{source})\) contains those conditions, and the display does not. Each component violates the blocks of its band, and each block's constraints must be cancelled by components of the sizes in its band, so the system couples overlapping bands along the whole scale range. Whether it has a solution is not decided here. The counts do not settle it: both the number of cancellation conditions and the number of free weights and local designs grow with the board.

Assessment and next step

Sheaf gluing on the matching site adds one genuinely new freedom: mixtures of explicitly constructed local designs whose errors cancel across restrictions. On the restriction poset without mixtures it is the recorded restriction method; unconstrained mixtures restate the problem; covers by subspace domains are the Mayer–Vietoris condition, which explains the recorded row obstruction and generalizes the recorded tree lemma but is vacuous for dense blocks. The dyadic test is reduced to the error-cancellation system above, which is the precise form of the Ó Conghaile-style lead for this source.

Next step. For odd-prime-clause-transfer, decide the error-cancellation system on its simplest nonvacuous case: two adjacent residual sizes and one block that is in the band for both. Before any computation, count its conditions and free parameters at the smallest board where both sizes lie in the stable range, as CLAUDE.md requires, and check whether the endpoint designs at the two sizes can differ on that block's constraints at all. If their errors are forced to agree up to scale, no mixture cancels them and the lead closes; otherwise the system is the object to study.

Verification gate. Searched the notebooks and claim index for the three new leads and for restriction mixtures; re-read the recorded tree-gluing lemma and row obstruction. A narrowly briefed fresh-context reviewer confirmed the pullback argument, the duality proof of (MX), the Mayer–Vietoris criterion as an equivalence over all pairwise-compatible families, and both examples, including the three-line dimension count. It required wording and scope corrections, all adopted: local spaces are spaces of functionals; unconstrained mixtures restate the problem only under the stated inclusion; the tree lemma is a sufficient condition with tree-edge agreement over \(\mathbb F_2\); the band width and its constant-rank assumption; corrected attributions for Porteous, Krajíček, Abramsky and topos approaches; and an allowed status. No computation was run.

Macaulay-quotient bounds cannot close the ternary window with the current separator; the dyadic band is eliminated additively

21 September 2026 · Conditional ceiling under the semi-regular model; application of recorded elimination · The window's width is set by the separator, not by the quotient bound. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question and counts first. The clique extension of the ternary graph criterion leaves, for random dense blocks, projected ranks in \([N/(4.4\times10^7),\ 1.6\times10^4N\Lambda]\), about \(39+\log_2\Lambda\) dyadic scales. The task was to bound the degree-\(k\) Macaulay quotient beyond degree-two heads, where the Boolean semi-regular model (compare the recorded relative Conjecture SR, a different, base-relative notion) predicts codimension about \(e^{-hk^2/s^2}\binom sk\) for \(h\) inputs. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. Following CLAUDE.md, before attempting a proof I compared what full success would give with what the window needs. That comparison decides the cycle: even the model's value leaves most of the window, because the constants that set the window belong to the separator. The requested quick error-cancellation check is in the last section; its simplest case turns out to be vacuous.

What any exponential quotient bound can reach

The criterion and its clique extension compare each block's reduction image with the share \(\binom sk e^{-5k^2/N}/(16(M+1))\) of the separated space, whose guaranteed dimension is \(\tfrac12e^{-5k^2/N}\binom sk\) for \(k=O(\sqrt{N\ln N})\).

(i) Arithmetic. Suppose a block of projected rank \(h\) has image at most \(A\binom sk\exp(-c\,hk^2/s^2)\) with constants \(A\ge1\), \(c>0\). This meets the share only if \[ h\ \ge\ \frac{s^2}{c}\left(\frac5N+\frac{\log(16A(M+1))}{k^2}\right)\ >\ \frac{1125N}{c}, \tag{MQ-ceiling} \] using \(s=15(N+1)\). The bound \(1125N/c\) holds for every \(k\): the gain \(hk^2/s^2\) and the separator's loss \(5k^2/N\) both scale with \(k^2\). At \(A=4\) the logarithm is exactly \(\Lambda\), and at the recorded \(k=\lceil\sqrt{N\Lambda}\rceil\) the threshold is at most \(6s^2/(cN)\approx1350N/c\). If the bound also credits the old relations, with image at most \(A\binom sk\exp(-\gamma k^2/N-c\,hk^2/s^2)\) for an old collision loss \(\gamma\), the same computation gives \(h\ge s^2((5-\gamma)/N+\Lambda/k^2)/c\).

(ii) No tuple beats the generic one. Fix \(k\) and the old space \(I_k(\Gamma_H)\). The dimension of the Macaulay space \(\operatorname{span}\{cg_i:\deg c\le k-2\}+I_k\) is the rank of a matrix whose entries are linear in the coefficients of \((g_1,\ldots,g_h)\). Its maximum is attained on a nonempty Zariski-open set of tuples over \(\overline{\mathbb F}_3\), and an \(\mathbb F_3\)-matrix has the same rank over both fields. So a block with \(h\) inputs has full codimension in \(\mathcal P_{\le k}\) at least that of a generic tuple of \(h\) polynomials of degree at most two, with the same old space. The comparison below is for random dense selector blocks with \(h\) inputs, whose projected rank is about \(h\). Selector blocks, whose top forms in \(\mathbb F_3[x]/(x_u^2)\) are squares \(\ell_i^2\) of linear forms, form a special family and can only do worse.

(iii) The model's value. For the Boolean semi-regular series \((1+t)^s(1+t^2)^{-h}\), a saddle-point estimate at \(t\approx k/s\) gives degree-\(k\) coefficient \(\binom sk\exp(-(1+o(1))hk^2/s^2)\) whenever \(hk/s^2\to0\). That holds throughout the window, since \(h=O(N)\) and \(k=O(\sqrt{N\log N})\). This is a heuristic derivation for the model series, not a proof about any block. In the model, \(c=1+o(1)\). The model ignores the old relations. The old quotient has dimension at most the matching-monomial count \(Z_k(G)\), heuristically about \(\binom sk e^{-0.93k^2/N}\), since each cell conflicts with about 28 others by row and hole. So the model's full codimension is about \(\binom sk e^{-0.93k^2/N-hk^2/s^2}\), that is, \(\gamma\approx0.93\). An exact check at \(s=3000\) confirms the regime. At \(k=40\) and \(80\), the coefficient ratio is between \(0.53e^{-x}\) and \(e^{-x}\) for \(x=hk^2/s^2\le3\). The first nonpositive coefficient, where the model quotient vanishes, lies beyond degree 400 for \(h\le800\), at 261 to 271 for \(h=3200\) (the two variants) and at 89 for \(h=12800\). Vanishing therefore needs \(h\) far above the window (table, script, both model variants \((1+t^2)^{-h}\) and \((1-t^2)^h\)).

Consequence. Under the model, any argument that charges each block its full Macaulay codimension in \(\mathcal P_{\le k}\) excludes random dense blocks only from about \(225(4.07+1)N\approx1140N\) up at the recorded \(k\), and from about \(915N\) up at every \(k\). The window becomes \([N/(4.4\times10^7),\ 1140N]\), a factor of about \(5\times10^{10}\) or 36 dyadic scales, instead of \(7\times10^{11}\Lambda\). The best possible quotient bound of this kind removes only about \(3.8+\log_2\Lambda\) scales. This extends the recorded absolute-head budget obstruction, which concerned disjoint-head estimates, to the generic codimension itself. It is conditional on the model for generic tuples. Unconditionally, only (i) and (ii) are proved.

What would close it. The remaining lever is the one isolated by the relative count: charge each block only its rank on \(W_k\), relative to the old normal-monomial count, instead of its full codimension. Suppose a separated space loses only \(e^{-ak^2/N}\) relative to that count, and blocks gain \(e^{-hk^2/s^2}\) relative to it. The dense threshold becomes about \(s^2(a/N+\Lambda/k^2)\). Meeting the low-rank reach \(N/(4.4\times10^7)\) then needs both \(a\lesssim5\times10^{-11}\) and \(k\gtrsim1.4\times10^5\sqrt{N\Lambda}\). The recorded guarantee gives only \(a\le5\), since its good monomials must also avoid the distinguished holes. Neither relative bound is proved, so this is the required size of a missing separator theorem, not a route.

Band blocks are eliminated additively

Keep the hypotheses of the criterion with its clique extension, but allow at most \(b\) arbitrary complete accuracy-one old-quadratic blocks, and replace \(TD+k\le N/10^6\) by \[ (2H_*+4R+2)(D+4b)+k\le N/10^6 . \] Then the source still has no PC refutation through \(D\). Proof. All blocks are level one: each removed block's inputs involve only board variables, so its fresh variables occur only in that block and its field equations, as Theorem 7.6 requires. The remaining system keeps Booleanity for the board variables and \(r^3-r\) for every remaining fresh variable. Historical Theorem 7.7 removes the \(b\) blocks one at a time, each at cost \((p-1)\delta=4\) for inputs \(1-L^2\). So a refutation through \(D\) yields one of the rest through \(D+4b\), which the criterion excludes at requested degree \(D+4b\ge5\). This is the recorded elimination-then-weight ledger with \(A=1\), \(C=4b\); It is also the pattern of the recorded reverse elimination over affine endpoints, which composes the same elimination with a downstream criterion. It is recorded as an application of both, not as a new claim.

The dyadic inventory. That inventory has one tuple per dyadic scale, so only its band is at issue. With \(b\) band blocks, the low reach falls to about \(N/(4\times10^6(11+4b))\), and the band has about \(\log_2(1.6\times10^4\Lambda\cdot4\times10^6(11+4b))+1\) scales. The fixed point is \(b\approx47\) to \(51\) and \(D+4b\approx200\) to \(216\) for \(\Lambda\) between 5 and 100. So, at the standard of the calibration argument and with the routine steps it lists, the criterion plus elimination handles the dyadic inventory. The recorded statements that the inventory defeats a common restriction and, through its band, the criterion alone remain true. The inventory no longer calibrates the combined method. A calibration for it needs more window blocks than elimination absorbs. An example is the thick dyadic inventory, with \(N\) independent random tuples at every scale: polynomially many blocks, about \(N\) times the number of band scales in the window.

The quick error-cancellation check

The sheaf entry asked about its simplest case: two adjacent residual sizes and one block in both bands, with counts first. The counts are as follows.

  • The criterion is nonvacuous only when \(TD+k\le N/10^6\) with \(T\ge2H_*\), \(H_*\approx k+(s/k)(\Lambda+5k^2/N)\approx91\sqrt{N\Lambda}\) and \(D=11\). That is \(2003\sqrt{N\Lambda}\le N/10^6\), or \(N\ge4.0\times10^{18}\Lambda\). Residual boards of both sizes must be at least this large, with \(k\ge2\times10^9\Lambda\) and designs of degree up to \(N/10^6\ge4\times10^{12}\Lambda\). No computation with actual designs is possible, so the question must be decided structurally.
  • One band block needs no mixture: the elimination above removes it at degree cost 4. More generally, taking \(R\) negligible, the budget absorbs up to about \(b_{\max}\approx\sqrt{N/\Lambda}/(7.3\times10^8)-11/4\) band blocks. So \(b_{\max}\ge1\) needs \(N\ge7.5\times10^{18}\Lambda\), about twice the nonvacuous threshold; at that threshold, \(b_{\max}=0\).

So the simplest case is vacuous. The mixture system matters only when more than \(b_{\max}\) blocks are in band, and then it faces the same missing implication as the kernel method: one design or weight for polynomially many window blocks with different input spans. The sheaf lead offers no mechanism for that yet. It stays parked, to be tested against the thick inventory if a mechanism appears.

Assessment and next step

The Macaulay line reached a model ceiling. Charging full quotient codimensions cannot close the window for random dense blocks even at the semi-regular value, because the separator's density loss grows at the same rate in \(k\) as the quotient's gain. The line's prospects through quotient bounds are weak. Closing the window through kernel counting would need a separated space nearly as large as the old normal-monomial count, and relative image bounds for general quadratic spans. The recorded separator is far from the first. The error-cancellation lead's simplest case is vacuous, and the dyadic inventory is handled by elimination, so the calibration is now the thick inventory.

Next step. For odd-prime-clause-transfer, run a route review of the ternary intermediate window. State the line's general claim, one weight for polynomially many window blocks. Test it against the thick dyadic inventory. Then decide between the relative-separator obligation, with the sizes above, and a mechanism that does not count codimensions.

Verification gate. Re-read the ternary criterion and its proof, the clique lemma and theorem with the dyadic calibration, the relative count, the separated-space lemma, the absolute-head budget, the elimination-then-weight ledger and historical Theorems 7.6 and 7.7. Claim searches covered semi-regularity, generic codimension, elimination composed with a criterion, calibration inventories and separator density. They found the related Conjecture SR and the reverse-elimination composition, now cited. One exact computation was run: the model-series table. A narrowly briefed fresh-context reviewer confirmed the (MQ-ceiling) algebra, the semicontinuity step, the saddle regime, the degree cost and the dyadic fixed point. It required seven corrections, all adopted: the old relations in the quotient (ceiling about \(1140N\) rather than \(1350N\)); the table bounds and both regularity variants; the nonvacuous board size \(4.0\times10^{18}\Lambda\) from \(T\ge2H_*\), instead of the weaker \(5.3\times10^{14}\Lambda\); the offset in \(b_{\max}\); the board-only inputs that Theorem 7.6 needs; the input-count scope; and the two citations. The corrections only weaken or relocate constants, so no second pass was run.

Route review: old-variable weights appear unable to handle the ternary window, and sign variables do not help

21 September 2026 · Route review of the ternary intermediate window · Falsification attempts; heuristic verdict on weight designs; next step makes it decisive. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

The line's general claim. For \(p=3\), every polynomial inventory of complete accuracy-one selector blocks on the separated graph admits a design built from the recorded mechanisms. Low-rank blocks use exact Fermat prefixes, affine cores use restriction kernels, dense and clique blocks use one common old-variable weight \(f\) in every block's degree-\(k\) Macaulay kernel, and a bounded band uses additive elimination. Together these would exclude the compiled source at degree \(11\). What the goal needs is exactly this, for arbitrary inventories, including polynomially many blocks of projected rank in the window \([N/(4.4\times10^7),\ \approx1140N]\), where none of these mechanisms applies. The calibration is the thick dyadic inventory, with \(N\) independent random tuples per dyadic scale. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The last five research entries on this item produced one extension (the clique class), one ceiling and three reductions of topological proposals to recorded mechanisms. None moved the window's general implication, which is why this entry is a review.

Falsification attempts

F1. Is the thick-inventory source easy? If it had a cheap refutation, the window would be moot. I found none, and found no mechanism that could produce one:

  • A complete accuracy-one block with its fields is satisfiable for every board assignment. Write the inputs as \(q_i=1-L_i^2\), with companions \(q_iP\) and \(P=1-\sum_jr_jq_j\). When every form \(L_i\) is nonzero, all \(q_i\) vanish and \(P=1\) satisfies the companions. Otherwise the fields \(r_j\) select one \(q_j=1\) and make \(P=0\). So the blocks act only as extension variables.
  • The one recorded block-level shortcut, the three-selector control, needs linearly dependent inputs. Over \(\mathbb F_3\) the four lines of a two-dimensional form space even satisfy \(\sum_\ell(1-\ell^2)=4-3A^2-3B^2=1\), which makes the block a tautology. Random forms in a block with \(h<s\) inputs are independent with high probability, so no such identity exists inside one block. Heuristically, for \(h<s\log2/\log1.5\approx1.71s\) the block's false set is a nonempty set of Boolean points of density about \((2/3)^h\); this is an expected count, not a proved concentration, and Boolean points are not \(\mathbb F_3\)-uniform. This covers only the bottom of the window, which reaches about \(76s\). Above about \(1.71s\), random blocks are expected to be tautologies on Boolean points, and the question there is only whether low degree sees it.
  • Identities among forms of different blocks abound, but companions of different blocks carry different products \(P_b\), and no recorded derivation combines them.

So the thick inventory stands as a calibration: its hardness is expected but unproved.

F2. Does a common weight fail in truth, or only in the bound? Heuristically, in truth. Let \(K_b\) be block \(b\)'s degree-\(k\) Macaulay kernel and \(W\) the recorded separated space, of dimension \(w\ge\tfrac12e^{-5k^2/N}\binom sk\). Since \(K_b\supseteq I_k\) and \(W\cap I_k=0\), general position must be taken in \(\mathcal P_{\le k}/I_k\). There, if the image of \(K_b\) is in general position with respect to \(W\), then \(\dim(K_b\cap W)=\max(0,w-\operatorname{codim}K_b)\). Under the semi-regular model with the old collision loss of the ceiling entry, the codimension of \(K_b\) modulo \(I_k\) is about \(\binom sk e^{-0.93k^2/N-hk^2/s^2}\). This exceeds \(w\) whenever \(h\lesssim915N\), at every \(k\). So a single random block of rank well inside the window is expected to leave no weight in \(W\), before any second block is added. For independent random dense tuples, general position is the natural expectation, since nothing aligns a random tuple's kernel with the matching monomials. Actual selector blocks \(1-\ell^2\) are a special family whose codimension is at most the generic one, so their kernels may be larger, which would favour weights. The recorded low- and dense-rank mechanisms are therefore not merely short of each other by weak bounds: under these two heuristics they miss the window intrinsically.

F3. Mixtures of weights. The error-cancellation system mixes designs, \(\Lambda=\sum_tw_t\lambda(f_t\,\sigma_t(\cdot))\). Under F2's heuristics no component's weight lies in a window block's kernel, so every component violates every window block, and all of those errors must cancel in the sum. Each window block contributes about \(\operatorname{codim}K_b\ge w\) independent error conditions (F2). One component has at most \(w\) free weight parameters. Heuristically, cancellation therefore needs more components than window blocks, and errors that are far from generic. Counting does not forbid this once there are enough components, but no recorded mechanism supplies the structure. The natural structured candidate is a product design. Give monomials with fresh support \(S\) the weight \(F_S=\prod_{b\in S}f_b\), substitute \(\beta_j=f_bc_j\) with \(\sum_jc_jq_j=f_b-E\), and apply \(\lambda\). A companion multiple \(\tilde m\,q_iP_b\) whose multiplier has fresh support \(S'\not\ni b\) then has value \(\lambda(F_{S'}\tilde m\,q_i)-\lambda(F_{S'}f_b\,\tilde m\,q_i\,f_b(f_b-E))=\lambda(F_{S'}\tilde m\,q_i(1-f_b^3+f_b^2E))\). Pointwise \(1-f_b^3=1-f_b\), which does not vanish. The single-weight method avoids this only because every term, including the support-\(S'\) term, carries the factor \(f_b\). This is the joint-feasibility failure of historical Lemma 6.6 and Example 6.5, in weight form.

F4. Can sign variables make the false set affine, as in characteristic two? Over \(\mathbb F_2\) a selector's false set \(\{L=1\}\) is an affine flat, and the affine-core kernel gains \(e^{-kH/s}\), linear in the rank. That is why the binary route has no window. Over \(\mathbb F_3\) the false set \(\{L^2=1\}\) is a union of two flats, and a block's false set is a union of \(2^h\) sign flats. Adding a Boolean sign variable \(\sigma\) with extension axiom \(L(L-1-\sigma)=0\) makes it affine, \(L=1+\sigma\), in the extended space. But \(\sigma\) is definable: \(\sigma:=L-L^2\) satisfies \(\sigma^2-\sigma=3L^2-3L+(L^4-L^2)-2(L^3-L)\) and \(L(L-1-\sigma)=L^3-L\). Both are Boolean consequences through degree four, since \(L^3=L\) on \(\mathbb F_3\)-values. So by substitution the extension costs at most a degree factor two, and adds no strength. Conversely, a degree-\(k\) kernel in the extended space pulls back to a Macaulay representation in \(x\) with multipliers of degree up to about \(2k\). On the flat \(\sigma\) is a function of \(x\), so the flat carries all functions of \(x\) and the extended image count gains nothing. The characteristic-two advantage is not reproducible by extension variables.

F5. Higher certificate degree. The weight method may use kernel certificates of degree \(K\) up to about \(T/2\), not only \(k\). Under the model, however, the Macaulay space gains no degree-\(\le k\) elements from larger \(K\) before the regularity degree. For \(h\) in the window that degree is heuristically at least about \(s^2/(12h)\ge N/60\) (see the table at \(s=3000\): beyond 400 for \(h\le800\), 261 to 271 at \(h=3200\), and 89 at \(h=12800\)). This is far beyond \(T\le N/10^7\).

Assessment of this line

The evidence is uniform. The ternary difficulty is the sign ambiguity \(L\in\{1,2\}\): it turns a block's false set into a union of flats, so every degree-bounded old-variable weight heuristically pays a quadratic rather than linear gain. The two recorded mechanisms, exact prefixes and weights, are both linear in \(N\) at the ends of the window and cannot meet. Mixtures have no recorded mechanism for cancellation, and sign variables are definable. The line's prospects, as a way to handle the window with old-variable weights, are weak. The verdict rests on two heuristics, the semi-regular model and general position. They are standard for random systems but unproved here, and they are the main remaining uncertainty. A second uncertainty is that actual selector blocks are special tuples whose kernels can exceed the generic ones. The binary balanced-rank obstruction is the analogous statement for random readers in the main thread; it concerns coverage after restriction, not weights, and is cited as a parallel, not a dependency.

Next step on the highest-risk item

Route item odd-prime-clause-transfer remains the highest risk. Make F2 decisive at one scale: for a random dense ternary tuple with \(h\) inputs well inside the window, say \(h=N\), prove that its degree-\(k\) Macaulay kernel meets the recorded \(W\) only in zero with high probability. Otherwise, exhibit the alignment that makes the intersection large. Either outcome decides the line. A proof shows that no old-variable weight design handles the window, and moves the route item to designs that are not weights, or to an argument that uses the derivation structure of actual Res(Lin) proofs. An alignment is precisely the missing mechanism. Before coding any finite analogue, count at the smallest parameters: the dimension of the matching-monomial span at degree \(k\), the codimension of one random block's kernel, and what general position predicts for their intersection. The test is nonvacuous only where the prediction lies strictly between zero and the trivial bound.

Verification gate. Re-read the ceiling entry, the ternary criterion's weight maps, historical Lemma 6.6 and Example 6.5, and the model table. Searches covered witness selectors for random dense blocks, general position of kernels, multi-weight designs and the binary-versus-ternary contrast. They found the binary dense-forms covering and balanced-rank results, cited as a parallel. No computation was run. A narrowly briefed fresh-context reviewer verified F4's identities and its no-gain argument. It required changes, adopted: the orientation of the block-satisfiability sentence; heuristic labels for the density and nonemptiness in F1, and the fact that F1 covers only the bottom of the window; general position taken modulo \(I_k\), making \(915N\) the primary figure; the special-tuple uncertainty for actual selector blocks; hedging in F2, F3 and the assessment; the regularity figure \(s^2/(12h)\) instead of \(s^2/(8h)\), which the table contradicted; and the claim note. One requested change was not adopted. The reviewer computed the F3 error as \(1-f_b^2\) from \(P(\beta)\) alone, but the product design also weights support-\((S'\cup\{b\})\) terms by \(f_b\), which gives \(1-f_b^3+f_b^2E\). The design is now defined explicitly so the computation can be checked.

Selector squares meet the good-matching space beyond general position in small graded tests

22 September 2026 · Finite check; mechanism unidentified · The general-position heuristic of the window review fails for selector squares at small scale. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question. The window route review concluded, under two heuristics, that one random window block leaves no old-variable weight in the separated space \(W\). The heuristics were the semi-regular model and general position of the block's Macaulay kernel relative to \(W\). Its next step asked to make this decisive, or to find an alignment. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. An exact asymptotic proof was out of reach this cycle. This cycle instead tests the general-position heuristic exactly, at the smallest sizes where the test is nonvacuous. The test controls for generic quadrics and for random subspaces. It asks whether actual selector squares \(\ell^2\) behave differently, which was the review's second uncertainty.

The test: a graded necessary condition

Let \(A=\mathbb F_3[y]/(y_u^2)\) on the nondistinguished cells, and let \(W\) be spanned by homogeneous degree-\(k\) good matching monomials. If \(f\in W\) lies in \(\operatorname{span}\{cg_i:\deg c\le k-2\}+I_k\), then comparing degree-\(k\) parts gives \[ f\in J_k=\sum_i\tau_iA_{k-2}+T_k , \] where \(\tau_i\) is the degree-two part of \(g_i\) and \(T_k\) is spanned by the old degree-two top forms times \(A_{k-2}\). In the Boolean multilinear ring, the degree-\(k\) part of \(cg\) is the \(A\)-product of the top parts when \(\deg c+\deg g=k\) and zero when \(\deg c+\deg g<k\), since repeated variables lower degree. This is the standard leading-form argument, the same device as the graded image in the binary two-form no-fall criterion. Hence \(W\cap J_k=0\) excludes every weight in \(W\) for that block; the converse is not claimed. For a selector \(1-\ell^2\), \(\tau\) is, up to sign, the top form of \(\ell^2\), namely \(2\sum_{u<v}a_ua_vy_uy_v\). The old top forms on the projected graph base are the same-row and same-hole cell pairs. Every monomial containing such a pair lies in \(T_k\), so the computation runs on matching monomials. The remaining old top forms are \(y_u\sum_{v\in\text{row }i}y_v\) for \(u\) in hole \(p_i\), and the product of the cell sums of two rows sharing a distinguished hole.

Counts and setup

We work in \(Q=A_k/T_k\), with \(q=\dim Q\), \(w'\) the dimension of \(W\)'s image, and \(\beta\) that of \(J_k\)'s image. General position predicts \(\dim(W\cap J)=\max(0,w'+\beta-q)\). The test is nonvacuous only where \(q-w'<\beta<q\), and the script sweeps \(h\) across that band. The graphs are random \(d\)-neighbor graph PHP with \(N\) holes and \(N+1\) rows. The four configurations are (degree-\(k\) matching monomials, \(q\), \(w'\)):

  • \(N=6\), \(d=4\), \(k=3\): 539, 238, 28;
  • \(N=8\), \(d=4\), \(k=3\): 1577, 969, 181;
  • \(N=8\), \(d=4\), \(k=4\): 4292, 1014, 84;
  • \(N=9\), \(d=4\), \(k=4\): 6738, 2678, 468.

The separation range of the recorded \(W\) is vacuous at these sizes; the test concerns only the linear-algebraic alignment of \(J_k\) with the span of good monomials. For each \(h\) the script compares three kinds of block: squares of uniform forms \(\ell\), uniform quadratic forms (generic), and a control that keeps the squares' \(J_k\) but replaces \(W\) by a uniform random subspace of dimension \(w'\). That control isolates whether the excess comes from the position of \(W\). Ranks are exact modulo 3, with random row compression only where rows exceed columns by more than 40. The per-job seeds are deterministic.

Results

  • Controls. At \(k=4\) the random-subspace control matches the prediction in all 140 trials, and generic quadrics in all 88 informative trials. Another 52 generic trials have \(\beta=q\) and match trivially. At \(k=3\) they match everywhere except two generic trials at zero gap (\(w'+\beta=q\)), where chance intersections over \(\mathbb F_3\) are expected.
  • Squares have smaller images. One square contributes 228 to 229 dimensions at \((N,d,k)=(8,4,4)\) and 297 to 298 at \((9,4,4)\), with occasional lower values, against about 255 and 325 for a generic quadric, inferred from \(\beta\) at the smallest \(h\) (\(511/2\) and \(1630/5\)). At equal \(h\), generic \(\beta\) always exceeds square \(\beta\). The shortfall of about \(s\) per form matches the relations \(\ell y_u\cdot\ell^2=0\), which hold because \(\ell^3=0\) in \(A\); in the Boolean ring \(\ell^3=\ell\).
  • Squares align beyond general position at \(k=4\). At \(k=3\) squares match the prediction in every trial. At \(k=4\) they exceed it in 27 of 80 trials at \(N=8\) and 4 of 60 at \(N=9\), by 1 to 27 dimensions. Of these, 17 at \(N=8\) (all with \(h\le4\)) and all 4 at \(N=9\) (with \(h\le7\)) occur at positive gaps \(q-w'-\beta\), up to 741, where a chance intersection is impossible. The other 10 at \(N=8\) are at \(h=5\), with a positive prediction exceeded by 1 to 15. In some trials a single good monomial lies in \(J_4\).

Mechanism checks, both negative or inconclusive.

  • Cells where every form vanishes: 15 of the 27 excess cases at \(N=8\) have none.
  • Single-generator products: no good monomial equals \(\ell_i^2\,y_ay_b\) for one form and one pair of its cells whose compatible support is the complementary pair.
  • Forms vanishing on every cell of a row occur in 89% of excess trials at \(N=8\), against 47% of the others. At \(N=9\) such forms are common in all trials. The intersection vectors are not concentrated on those rows.

An independent implementation by the reviewer reproduces the strongest case exactly (\(q=1014\), \(w'=84\), \(\beta=899\), intersection 27 against a prediction of 0). It works in the full \(A_4\) with all 17550 monomials, builds its own old top forms and uses exact elimination without projection. The code, raw results, analysis scripts and that check, with outputs, are retained.

Assessment and next step

At \(k=4\), selector squares meet the good-matching space more than general position predicts, while generic quadrics and random subspaces do not. So, for this graded necessary condition at these sizes, general position is not a safe model for selector blocks. Its second uncertainty, that special tuples could have larger kernels relative to \(W\), is realized at small scale, in the direction that favours weights. The evidence is limited. The frequency and size of the excess fall from \(N=8\) to \(N=9\), consistent with a small-size effect, and only two sizes at one degree beyond three were tested. The mechanism is unidentified, and the graded condition is only necessary: an excess in \(J_k\) need not give an actual kernel element with lower-order terms. Next step: identify the mechanism from the single-monomial cases, by extracting a minimal generating combination, and derive a local criterion for a good monomial to lie in \(J_k\). Then decide from that criterion whether the alignment survives for dense random forms at \(s=15N\) or is a small-support effect. Only a surviving mechanism that is common to many blocks would give weights. The review's window verdict stands until then, but it is no longer decisive.

Verification gate. Re-read the window review, the ternary criterion's kernel condition and the projected old relations. Searched the record for graded or leading-form kernel tests; it gives the binary two-form criterion, cited. The computations ran on 14 worker processes with deterministic seeds. The first two runs used an older script version and non-reproducible seeds, and are superseded by the retained runs. A narrowly briefed fresh-context reviewer reviewed the code line by line and found no artifact: the old top forms are complete, and the kinds differ only in the form used. It independently recomputed the strongest case in the full graded space with its own elimination, reproducing every number. Its eight wording and scoping changes were adopted: the control's construction, the informative-trial counts, the source of the generic per-form figures, the syzygy statement and the sign, the degree condition in the leading-form step, the split of the excess tallies, and scoping the assessment to the graded condition at these sizes.

The selector alignment is a row collapse of the old quotient, and disappears at five neighbors in a small test

22 September 2026 · Finite check with an explicit mechanism; heuristic scaling · The excess disappears at five neighbors per row. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question. The graded alignment test found selector squares meeting the good-matching space beyond general position at degree four, and left the mechanism open. If the mechanism survived on the recorded sixteen-neighbor graph, it would be exactly what the window review said an alignment would have to be: a way for weights to beat counting. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. This cycle identifies the mechanism and tests its predicted scaling.

Localization

The analysis covers every excess trial of the test at \((N,d,k)=(8,4,4)\) and \((9,4,4)\). For each, it lists the good monomials \(y_S\) lying in \(J_4\), and checks whether one form's square, or a pair of squares, already puts \(y_S\) there. At \(N=8\), 10 of the 17 excess trials with \(h\le4\) have single good monomials in \(J_4\), 1 to 7 per trial. In seven of them one form suffices. Counting also \(h=5\), there are 21 single-form cases. At \(h=5\) most of \(W\) lies in \(J_4\) (58 to 84 of 84 good monomials), as general position already predicts. No excess trial at \(N=9\) has a single good monomial in \(J_4\). Greedy deletion then finds a minimal set of multipliers for each single-form case. Their sizes range from 1 to 57; five have two elements (scripts and outputs).

The mechanism in one case

Take \(S=\{14,15,20,21\}\), the cells \((4,0),(5,3),(6,4),(7,6)\) as (row, hole), with multipliers \(y_{14}y_{21}\) and \(y_{14}y_{23}\). Cells 21 and 23 are two of the three cells of row 7; its third cell is 22, at \((7,0)\). Row 7's distinguished hole is 2, which contains cells 9 and 18. The old quotient has the projected relation \[ y_u\,(y_{21}+y_{22}+y_{23})\in T\qquad(u\text{ in hole }2), \] the top form of \(x_{7,2}\,y_u=0\) with \(x_{7,2}=1-\sum_{\text{row }7}y\). The expansion of \(\ell^2y_{14}y_{21}\) modulo collisions has terms \(y_{14}y_{21}y_cy_d\) with \(\{c,d\}\) among \(\{9,15\},\{9,16\},\{9,20\},\{15,18\},\{15,20\},\{16,18\}\). The expansion of \(\ell^2y_{14}y_{23}\) has \(\{9,16\},\{9,20\},\{16,18\}\) with the same coefficients.

  • Each common term pairs up. For example, \(y_9y_{14}y_{16}(y_{21}+y_{23})\equiv-y_9y_{14}y_{16}y_{22}\equiv0\), because cell 22 shares hole 0 with cell 14.
  • The unpaired terms containing a hole-2 cell vanish by the same relation. For example, \(y_9y_{14}y_{15}y_{21}\equiv0\), because cells 22 and 23 collide with 14 and 15.

What remains is \(2\,y_{14}y_{15}y_{20}y_{21}=2y_S\). So \(y_S\) lies in \(J_4\) through one square and two multipliers. Three of the other four two-multiplier cases have the same shape: two multipliers differing in one cell of a row, whose remaining cells are blocked by collisions with the monomial. The fourth, \(S=\{1,9,14,24\}\) with multipliers \(\{5,14\}\) and \(\{9,14\}\), pairs cells of two different rows and was not analyzed. The larger minimal sets were not analyzed; they presumably chain the same collapse, but that is unverified.

What the mechanism is. The relation \(y_u\sum_{\text{row }i}y\) with \(u\) in hole \(p_i\) is the projected form of the row equation \(\sum_jX_{ij}=1\). It is the class that the sheaf entry identified as the recorded row obstruction in \(H_1\). When every other cell of row \(i\) is blocked by the monomial, it collapses a sum over the row to a single term. In the four analyzed cases, squares of forms reduce to single good monomials because their terms pair up across two multipliers that differ within one row.

Predicted scaling and its test

Heuristic. Each row has \(d-1\) cells. A collapse needs a row whose cells, apart from the two carrying the paired multipliers, are all blocked by the monomial: \(d-3\) cells, whose holes are random. The probability of that is roughly \((k/N)^{d-3}\) per row, up to polynomial factors. At \(d=4\), \(N=8\), \(k=4\), only one cell needs blocking and this is large. On the recorded sixteen-neighbor graph with \(k=O(\sqrt{N\log N})\) it is about \((k/N)^{13}\), which vanishes polynomially. This is a per-row, per-monomial probability. It does not bound the number of monomials and multiplier pairs, which is large, and it does not cover the unanalyzed larger minimal sets. It therefore predicts that collapsing configurations form a small fraction, not that they are absent. The prediction is that the excess alignment is a small-degree artifact, and that it already drops at \(d=5\), where two cells per row need blocking.

Test at \(d=5\). The same test ran at \((N,d,k)=(8,5,4)\): \(s=36\), 13628 matching monomials, \(q=5590\), \(w'=178\), \(h=9,\ldots,13\), with 16 square trials per \(h\) and 4 of each control. All 80 square trials match general position, 64 of them at positive gaps and 16 inside the band \(q-w'<\beta<q\). At \(d=4\) with the same \(N\) and \(k\), 27 of 80 trials exceeded it. Both controls match in all 40 trials. So one more cell per row removed the excess at this size, as the blocking count predicts. The evidence is one graph (seed 7) at one \((N,k)\). The \(d=4\) comparison used a different graph (seed 5) with 20 square trials per \(h\). The computation uses a new bit-sliced GF(3) elimination in C (gf3.c), which passes a self-test against the NumPy reference: exhaustive rank cases, plus randomized reduced-echelon and row-space checks. It also reproduces all 24 recorded trials of a check configuration at \((8,4,4)\) exactly. The earlier NumPy run of this configuration was killed for low system memory before saving anything; its normal-form step in alignment.py was changed to work in row chunks without changing results, and the reported \(d=5\) run used alignment_fast.py.

Assessment and next step

The only alignment found between selector squares and the good-matching space is a collapse through the row relation, and it needs rows whose cells a monomial can block. It disappeared at five neighbors per row in the one test run, and the blocking heuristic predicts it becomes a small fraction on the recorded sixteen-neighbor graph. The window review's verdict against old-variable weights in the window therefore stands again, with this second uncertainty tested at small scale. Next step (odd-prime-clause-transfer): take the review's route decision. Weights are excluded heuristically, and the sheaf candidate on subspace contexts runs into the recorded subspace wall. So the remaining alternative is the derivation structure of actual Res(Lin) proofs, whose lines are not an arbitrary inventory. Search the record for proof-order design constructions and line-by-line invariants before formulating one, then test it against the thick inventory. That inventory is not derivable, so it cannot calibrate a derivation-aware method.

Sheaf check

The one nontrivial relation that produced extra weights here is the recorded row class. It acts only through local blocking, which the sixteen-neighbor graph makes negligible. No presheaf with a new vanishing or gluing property has appeared. The row class is the only \(H_1\) element that any computation has so far shown to matter. It enlarges the kernels available to weights only while rows are small enough to be blocked, so it gives no mechanism at the recorded graph degree. The natural presheaf in which a Res(Lin) line is local assigns to each bounded-dimension space of linear forms a joint value distribution, compatible under restriction, in the manner of sheaf-theoretic contextuality. Its sections would amount to PHP consistency under linear constraints of high rank. That is the recorded subspace wall: recorded and published techniques stop at rank of order \(n\). A cycle on that presheaf would have to start from the wall, not rediscover it.

Verification gate. Re-read the alignment entry, the window review and the projected old relations. The record search for subspace local-consistency objects found the main notebook's subspace wall, cited in the sheaf check. A narrowly briefed fresh-context reviewer checked the C library, its wrapper and the fast driver line by line. It reran the self-test, confirmed that the driver reproduces the 24 recorded trials, verified the worked mechanism with its own script, and confirmed every tally. It required six wording changes, all adopted: the two-row fourth case, the heuristic label and fraction scope of the scaling, the single-graph scope of the \(d=5\) evidence, "most" at \(h=5\), the self-test description, and the unused configuration. The first minimal-subset search timed out, because it rebuilt bases per pair and its runtime was not estimated. The first \(d=5\) attempt was killed for low system memory. Both were replaced by the optimized versions retained here.
