Thread route review: bounded-depth closure for unary PHP would need a new method; its first test is a danger notion measured on forced cells

22 September 2026 · Route review of the odd-prime thread · Window weak; closure sub-line weak, payoff limited to bounded depth. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

The thread's general claim. Superpolynomial lower bounds for \(\mathrm{Res}(\mathrm{lin}_{\mathbb F_p})\) refutations of unary PHP, at every odd prime, follow by compiling a refutation into complete selector blocks and excluding the compiled source. What the goal needs is the case the statement set leaves open: refutations with more than \(Cn\) window lines, of nonlocal dimension above \(n^{1/(p-1)-\varepsilon}\). The last thread review found one outside mechanism that handles such lines in DAG-like proofs of bounded depth, the closure method of Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson and of Byramji and Impagliazzo. Two cycles tested it for unary PHP: the one-defect analysis and the column dichotomy. Route items under review: all three, with the closure sub-line of the first.

Falsification attempt: does the method transfer to unary PHP?

The method has three parts: a safety notion with pigeon rows as blocks, a probability bound for safe systems under a hard distribution, and a restriction step that implies a safe system while keeping PHP hard on the free rows. Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson's path argument also needs the negation of every axiom to be locally inconsistent: no solution may be injective on the closure. For unary PHP each part now has a recorded obstruction.

  1. Safety. Over \(\mathbb F_p\) with \(p\) odd, the equation \(x_{i_1j}+x_{i_2j}=2\) has rank one, and every \(0/1\) solution puts both pigeons in hole \(j\). A single nonzero form is never dangerous, so this system is safe with pigeon rows as blocks. Its closure is empty, so it is locally consistent although it falsifies a hole clause, and every restriction implying it falsifies that clause. The same holds for the rank-two system \(\{x_{i_1j}=1,\ x_{i_2j}=1\}\), whose two independent forms have support in two rows. In the bit encoding over \(\mathbb F_p\), a system of forms supported on the two rows that fixes both labels needs at least \(\lceil2l/(p-1)\rceil\) independent forms, since a system of rank \(r\) with a \(0/1\) solution forces at most \(r(p-1)\) bits (shown below). It is therefore dangerous once \(l\ge p\), and the negated hole clause itself, with \(2l\) forms, is dangerous once \(l\ge2\). This is an elementary remark, checked below.
  2. Probability. By the column dichotomy, a bound that charges the occupancy forms is incompatible with linear search hardness on every board, at every prime.
  3. Exemption. Exempting the occupancy forms as Byramji and Impagliazzo exempt column sums is blocked by safety for fixed \(p\). Under the modular-collision distribution conditioned on its empty set, the \(n-p+1\) occupancy forms outside that set are fixed, and a safe system has room for at most \(p\) further forms beside them. Without conditioning, the room is one form.

So for fixed \(p\) the method does not transfer as is. What would be needed is a new closure method for the unary encoding: a new danger notion, a closure lemma, a probability bound, a restriction step and a hard distribution. Byramji and Impagliazzo give their own reasons, in Remark A.4, for working with a block-lifted unary PHP; the obstructions above are consistent with them.

Assessment of each route item

  • odd-prime-clause-transfer, the window: weak, unchanged. No batched mechanism is recorded, and the one recorded outside mechanism does not transfer as is.
  • odd-prime-clause-transfer, the closure sub-line: weak. Its prospects rest on designing a new closure method for the unary encoding. Its payoff is limited to bounded depth. Full success would give the first statement in this record that admits arbitrarily many window lines at an odd prime, but only for refutations of bounded depth, which is still a restriction and not the goal. It is the only recorded candidate that could handle more than \(Cn\) window lines, if it can be built.
  • same-graph-composition: bookkeeping; nothing open.
  • scope-and-review: complete up to external review. The write-up of the statement set, and the audit of the binary theorem's CNF compiler in the main notebook, await user decisions.

The first test of a unary closure notion

Obstruction 1 refutes the pigeon-row notion, and more generally any notion that depends only on the span and does not flag the single form \(x_{i_1j}+x_{i_2j}\). The alternative chosen here is to measure danger on forced cells. A system forces a cell when all its \(0/1\) solutions agree on that cell.

Lemma (forced cells). Over \(\mathbb F_p\), a linear system of rank \(r\) in \(0/1\) variables that has a \(0/1\) solution forces at most \(r(p-1)\) variables.

Proof. Let \(x^*\) be a \(0/1\) solution, choose \(r\) independent forms that span the system's forms, and let \(c_t\in\mathbb F_p^r\) be the column of variable \(t\). Flipping \(t\) changes the form values by \(+c_t\) if \(x^*_t=0\) and by \(-c_t\) if \(x^*_t=1\). Suppose \(r(p-1)+1\) variables were forced. By Olson's theorem, the Davenport constant of \(\mathbb F_p^r\) is \(r(p-1)+1\), so every sequence of that length, repeats and zeros allowed, has a nonempty subsequence summing to zero. Some nonempty set of the forced variables therefore has signed columns summing to zero, and flipping all of them gives another \(0/1\) solution. That contradicts forcing. \(\square\)

Collisions and empty pigeons are the forced patterns to forbid, so a notion must charge rows and holes together. A charge on rows alone lets a collision through, and a charge on holes alone lets an empty pigeon through. For the forced cells \(\{(i_1,j),(i_2,j)\}\) of the collision system, the minimal vertex covers are \(\{\text{hole }j\}\) and \(\{\text{rows }i_1,i_2\}\). They are incomparable, and each makes the negated hole clause locally inconsistent, since no solution sends \(i_1\) and \(i_2\) to distinct holes or leaves at most one pigeon in \(j\). So a closure made of covers needs a canonical rule. A heuristic warning goes with this. Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson's closure theory rests on their Theorem 3.1, a Rado-type min-max, which holds whenever each form is charged to one block of any family, overlapping or not. A matching charge takes a row and a hole together, which is an intersection of three matroids. No general min-max theorem is known for that, and the problem is NP-hard in general.

The candidate to test is an iterated forced-cell closure, taken modulo the occupancy span. Let \(O\) be the occupancy equations fixed by the modular-collision distribution conditioned on its empty set \(E\): \(\mathrm{col}_h=1\) for \(h\notin E\), and every cell of \(E\) zero. For a system \(\Phi\), count its rank as \(\dim(\langle\Phi\rangle+\langle O\rangle)-\dim\langle O\rangle\). Count its forced cells as those forced by \(\Phi\cup O\) but not by \(O\) alone. Start with the rows and holes of those cells. Substitute values for them from a solution, recompute the cells forced in the residual system, add their rows and holes, and repeat until nothing new is forced. One-shot covers already have size at most \(r(p-1)\) without \(O\), by the Lemma. So the test concerns the iteration, and \(O\): the Lemma is proved without \(O\), and whether a bound linear in the rank survives modulo \(O\) is part of the test. The test ends in one of three ways. The closure may depend on the substituted solution with no canonical choice. It may fail to be monotone under weakening. Or it may exceed any constant times the rank. Any one of these closes this candidate, not the whole sub-line. If none happens, the next obligations are a restriction step for systems of rank up to \(cn\), then the probability bound and the search hardness for the modular-collision distribution on a bounded-degree graph.

Next step

Next step (odd-prime-clause-transfer): test the iterated forced-cell closure modulo the occupancy span. Read Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson's Sections 3 to 5 exactly and state the analogues of their uniqueness, monotonicity and size bound for it. Then prove them, or find an example where the closure has no canonical choice, is not monotone, or grows faster than the rank. The first check is whether the Lemma's bound survives modulo \(O\).

Sheaf check

Rows as blocks glue local sections pigeon by pigeon, and a collision forced by a single equation is a section that nothing forbids. A closure that forbids it must see the forced cells, which depend on the values of the forms and not only on their supports. It must also treat a pigeon and a hole as one gluing step. The fixed occupancy forms remain a global section that the gluing must be measured against.

Verification gate. Re-read verbatim: Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson's Sections 1.3 and 3 to 4 (safety, Theorem 3.1, closure, Lemmas 4.7 and 4.9, local consistency and the path argument), and the column dichotomy for obstructions 2 and 3. Record searches for safe systems, unary rows and blocks, hole clauses, restriction and danger, and for Olson, Davenport and forced cells, found no earlier forced-cell bound or unary closure notion. The nearest record, Corollary SL, concerns label bits over \(\mathbb F_2\). Olson's theorem is imported. Two fresh-context reviews:

  • First pass. Verdict: gap. The draft proposed a danger notion on supports, charged by matchings. The reviewer showed that over \(\mathbb F_p\) a rank-one equation forces a collision, so any notion on supports passes it. The reviewer supplied the forced-cell bound through Olson's theorem. It also showed that the draft's growth test was wrong, since Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson's own closure can jump by many rows with one form; their total size bound is the right analogue. It required qualifying "does not transfer", the bit comparison and two claims about the sources. The first-test section was rewritten.
  • Second pass. The rewrite added the forced-cell bound and the non-uniqueness example, so a second reviewer checked them. Verdict: sound with fixes. The flipping proof and the bit comparison are correct. The fixes were these: the bound needs a \(0/1\) solution; supports fail only for notions that depend on the span; the covers in the example must be vertex covers of the forced cells; the min-max remark is a heuristic; and the test needed one concrete candidate, a precise meaning of "modulo the occupancy span" and a stated end. These fixes only weaken or sharpen claims, so no third pass was run.

No computation was run.

Forced-cell closures for unary PHP: the forced-cell bound survives modulo the occupancy equations, but forcing cannot define local consistency

22 September 2026 · Working proof of the bound, every prime; counterexample to forced-cell closures, for unary PHP over \(\mathbb F_p\), \(p\) odd. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The route review proposed testing an iterated forced-cell closure for unary PHP over \(\mathbb F_p\), taken modulo the occupancy equations of the modular-collision distribution. Its first check was whether the bound of Lemma (forced cells), at most \(r(p-1)\) forced cells for rank \(r\), survives modulo those equations. Then the closure had to be tested for a canonical choice, monotonicity and a size bound. The test ends when the candidate passes, or when one of these fails. A failure closes this candidate, not the closure sub-line.

What the closure is for

Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson's path argument uses the closure through local consistency. A system is locally consistent if some solution is injective on its closure. Two properties are needed.

  • Leaves. The negation of every axiom is locally inconsistent.
  • Delayer step. If \(\Phi\) is locally consistent and its rank is small, then for every form \(f\) some value \(\alpha\) keeps \(\Phi\wedge(f=\alpha)\) locally consistent.

For a forced-cell closure, local consistency reads as follows. \(\Phi\) together with the occupancy equations has a \(0/1\) solution, the cells forced to \(1\) form a partial matching, and no pigeon has all its cells forced to \(0\). The leaf property then holds for hole and pigeon clauses.

The bound modulo the occupancy equations

Let \(G\) be a bipartite graph between pigeons and holes. Let the variables be its cells \(x_{ih}\), with values in \(\{0,1\}\). For each hole \(h\), let \(\mathrm{col}_h\) be the sum of the cells of column \(h\), and let \(O\) be the equations \(\mathrm{col}_h=b_h\) with fixed \(b_h\in\mathbb F_p\). For a linear system \(\Phi\), its rank modulo \(O\) is \(\dim(\langle\Phi\rangle+\langle\mathrm{col}\rangle)-\dim\langle\mathrm{col}\rangle\).

Lemma (forced cells modulo occupancy). Let \(p\) be any prime. Suppose \(\Phi\cup O\) has a \(0/1\) solution and \(\Phi\) has rank \(r\) modulo \(O\). Then at most \(r\,p\,(p-1)\) cells are forced by \(\Phi\cup O\) without being forced by \(O\) alone.

Proof. Let \(x^*\) be a \(0/1\) solution of \(\Phi\cup O\). Choose forms \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\) with \(\langle\Phi\rangle+\langle\mathrm{col}\rangle=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_r\rangle\oplus\langle\mathrm{col}\rangle\). A \(0/1\) assignment \(y\) solves \(\Phi\cup O\) exactly when it satisfies \(O\) and \(g(y)=g(x^*)\): each form of \(\Phi\) is a combination of the \(g_k\) and the column forms, and conversely. For a cell \(t\) let \(c_t\in\mathbb F_p^r\) be its coefficients in \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\) and \(\sigma_t=1-2x^*_t\in\{\pm1\}\). Flipping a set \(U\) of cells changes \(g\) by \(\sum_{t\in U}\sigma_tc_t\) and \(\mathrm{col}_h\) by \(\sum_{t\in U\cap\mathrm{col}\,h}\sigma_t\). Let \(F\) be the set of cells forced by \(\Phi\cup O\) but not by \(O\) alone, and \(H_F\) the set of holes whose columns meet \(F\).

  1. Few columns. For each \(h\in H_F\) pick \(t_h\in F\) in column \(h\). Since \(O\) alone does not force \(t_h\), some \(0/1\) solution \(y^h\) of \(O\) differs from \(x^*\) at \(t_h\). Let \(U_h\) be the set of cells of column \(h\) where \(y^h\) and \(x^*\) differ. Then \(t_h\in U_h\), \(\sum_{t\in U_h}\sigma_t=b_h-b_h=0\), and we set \(v_h=\sum_{t\in U_h}\sigma_tc_t\in\mathbb F_p^r\). The Davenport constant of \(\mathbb F_p^r\) is \(r(p-1)+1\) (Olson). If \(|H_F|\ge r(p-1)+1\), some nonempty \(S\subseteq H_F\) has \(\sum_{h\in S}v_h=0\). The sets \(U_h\) lie in distinct columns, so flipping \(\bigcup_{h\in S}U_h\) keeps \(O\) and \(g\), and gives a solution that differs from \(x^*\) at every \(t_h\), \(h\in S\). That contradicts forcing, so \(|H_F|\le r(p-1)\).
  2. Few cells. For \(t\in F\) let \(w_t=\sigma_t\,(e_{h(t)},c_t)\in\mathbb F_p^{H_F}\times\mathbb F_p^r\), where \(h(t)\) is the hole of \(t\). If \(|F|\ge(|H_F|+r)(p-1)+1\), Olson's theorem gives a nonempty \(T\subseteq F\) with \(\sum_{t\in T}w_t=0\). Flipping \(T\) changes every \(\mathrm{col}_h\) by \(0\) and \(g\) by \(0\). That again contradicts forcing. So \(|F|\le(|H_F|+r)(p-1)\le(r(p-1)+r)(p-1)=r\,p\,(p-1)\). \(\square\)

The right-hand sides \(b_h\) are arbitrary, so the Lemma covers the modular-collision distribution conditioned on its empty set \(E\): \(b_h=1\) outside \(E\), with the cells of \(E\) deleted. The first check passes. The constant rises from \(p-1\) to \(p(p-1)\).

Forcing cannot define local consistency

Example. Take distinct pigeons \(1,2,3\) and a hole \(a\), on any graph in which \(a\) has at least \(p\) further neighbours and every other hole has at least two neighbours, for instance the full board with at least \(p+3\) pigeons. Let \[ \Phi=\{x_{1a}+x_{2a}+x_{3a}=2\}, \] with the occupancy equations \(\mathrm{col}_h=1\). The three cells hold \(0/1\) values, so their sum lies in \(\{0,1,2,3\}\). It is \(2\) modulo \(p\) only when it equals \(2\), because \(2-p<0\) and \(2+p>3\). So every solution puts exactly two of the pigeons \(1,2,3\) in \(a\), a collision. Yet \(\Phi\cup O\) forces no cell. Any two of the three cells can be the ones, and any \(p-1\) of the at least \(p\) further neighbours of \(a\) then make its occupancy \(p+1\), so no further cell of \(a\) is forced either. The rank of \(\Phi\) modulo \(O\) is one.

  • One-shot closure. \(\Phi\wedge(x_{1a}=1)\) has rank \(2\) and one forced cell, \(1a\), so by the reading above it is locally consistent. Now take \(f=x_{2a}\). For \(\alpha=1\), cells \(1a\) and \(2a\) are forced to \(1\), a collision. For \(\alpha=0\), cell \(3a\) is forced to \(1\), and \(1a\), \(3a\) collide. No other value has a \(0/1\) solution. So no \(\alpha\) keeps local consistency.
  • Iterated closure. Iteration adds matching propagation: a cell forced to \(1\) sets the rest of its row and column to \(0\). \(\Phi\) forces nothing, so it is locally consistent. Take \(f=x_{1a}\). For \(\alpha=1\), propagation sets \(x_{2a}=x_{3a}=0\), and the equation fails. For \(\alpha=0\), cells \(2a\) and \(3a\) are forced to \(1\). So the Delayer step fails already at rank one.

Both forced-cell candidates are canonical. The one-shot one is also monotone, and by the Lemma it has size at most \(2rp(p-1)\) rows and holes beyond those forced by \(O\). Neither supports the Delayer step, so both are refuted. The reason is that a rank-one equation can force a collision without forcing any cell.

Any workable notion must reject such systems. Suppose a notion of local consistency has four properties. Locally consistent systems have a \(0/1\) solution. The notion is monotone under implication over \(0/1\) points. It has the leaf property. It supports the Delayer step for systems of rank below \(m\). Let \(\Phi\) be a system whose forms are supported on \(m\) given cells, all of whose \(0/1\) solutions contain a collision among those cells. If \(\Phi\) were locally consistent, querying the \(m\) cells one at a time would keep local consistency while fixing all of them. The rank stays at most \(m\), and each answer is the value at a \(0/1\) solution. The fixed values would then be a \(0/1\) solution of \(\Phi\) on those cells, which contains a collision. So the system would imply the negation of a hole clause over \(0/1\) points, which monotonicity and the leaf property forbid. So \(\Phi\) must be locally inconsistent. If local consistency asks for a solution that is a matching on the closure, the closure must see a collision in every solution. In the example this means containing \(a\), or rows of which every solution puts two into \(a\), for instance \(1,2,3\).

Calibration. For \(p\ge5\), such collisions can spread over many holes. For \(2\le k\le p-2\), take \(k\) holes \(h_1,\ldots,h_k\), each with two designated pigeons out of \(2k\) distinct pigeons. Let each hole have at least \(2p\) further neighbours, and every other hole at least two neighbours. Take the equation that the sum of the \(2k\) designated cells is \(k+1\). The sum lies in \(\{0,\ldots,2k\}\), with \(k+1-p<0\) and \(k+1+p>2k\), so exactly \(k+1\) designated cells are one and some \(h_j\) holds two designated pigeons. No cell is forced, since any \(k+1\) of the \(2k\) cells, with \(2k-1\ge k+1\), can be the ones. For each \(j\), some solution doubles \(h_j\) and puts one designated pigeon in each other hole. It adds \(p-1\) further neighbours of \(h_j\), of its choice, gives the other designated holes no further pigeon, and puts exactly one pigeon in every remaining hole. Its only collisions are in \(h_j\). A closure that sees a collision in all these solutions must, for each \(j\), contain \(h_j\), or both designated pigeons of \(h_j\), or all but at most \(p-2\) of the further neighbours of \(h_j\). The last option costs at least \(p+2\) rows. So the closure has at least \(\min(k,p+2)=k\) rows and holes, and one equation already needs at least \(p-2\). For comparison, the Lemma's bound on forced cells is \(r\,p\,(p-1)\).

What local consistency needs instead

In Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson's argument the Delayer step rests on freedom outside the closure: with the closure fixed, a safe system constrains at most one bit per pigeon, so any few further pigeons can be placed injectively. The example shows that forcing does not measure this freedom for unary PHP over \(\mathbb F_p\). The proposal is to measure extendability. Call \(\Phi\) free outside \(C\), for a set \(C\) of rows and holes, when every partial matching of a few pigeons outside \(C\) into holes outside \(C\) extends to a solution of \(\Phi\cup O\) in which each placed pigeon has the rest of its row zero. Without that row condition every system would be free outside the empty set. Local consistency would ask for a solution that is a matching on a closure \(C\) of size \(O_p(\text{rank})\) outside which \(\Phi\) is free. Freedom alone does not settle the example. With two extra pigeons, \(\{a\}\) is not enough: placing pigeons \(1\) and \(2\) outside \(a\) would force \(x_{3a}=2\). The requirement that \(\Phi\) be locally inconsistent comes from the rejection argument above, not from freedom. The notion is therefore a proposal whose details, including how local consistency uses \(C\), decide whether it works. The Delayer avoids the example by choosing another value, for instance \(0\), when the form is first queried.

Assessment

The candidate named by the route review is refuted, and the sub-line continues with a sharper requirement. The bound modulo the occupancy equations is a usable tool. The open question is now whether a closure of size \(O_p(\text{rank})\) outside which the system is free exists for unary PHP over \(\mathbb F_p\). For \(p\ge5\), single equations already force collisions spread over up to \(p-2\) holes. That is consistent with a bound linear in the rank for fixed \(p\), but it is the kind of spreading a proof must control. The payoff remains a bounded-depth endpoint, not the goal, and the window's prospects are unchanged.

Sheaf check

Local consistency is a gluing condition: a section on the closure, a matching, must extend over the rest. Forcing measures only sections that are unique. The example has no unique section on any cell, and still no section that is a matching on its three pigeons and one hole. The obstruction is a failure to extend, not a forced value, so the closure must be defined by extension.

Next step

Next step (odd-prime-clause-transfer): define the extendability closure exactly. Fix the number of extra pigeons, the treatment of the occupancy equations and a canonical choice. Then try to prove a size bound of the form \(C_p\cdot\text{rank}\) by zero-sum arguments like the Lemma's, or find a rank-one family whose closure must grow with \(n\). The calibration family is the first test case, and the Delayer step on the example is the second.

Verification gate. Re-read verbatim: Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson's Sections 1.3.3 and 4 (local consistency, the weakening and resolution steps, the Delayer step, Lemma 4.7), and the route review's Lemma and candidate. Before the proof was drafted, a record check was run on the Lemma's statement. It found only the route review's Lemma, which proves the bound without the occupancy equations and lists this case as open. Olson's theorem is imported. My first draft of the example used \(x_{1a}+x_{2a}+x_{3b}+x_{4b}=3\), which fails at \(p=3\) because the all-zero assignment also has sum \(0\equiv3\). It was replaced by the single-hole example before review, and the four-cell pattern survives as the case \(k=2\) of the calibration. A fresh-context reviewer checked the entry. Verdict: sound with fixes. The Lemma's proof was confirmed, and it holds for every prime. The fixes:

  • With exactly \(p-1\) further neighbours of \(a\), the further cells are forced and the example collapses. It now requires \(p\) further neighbours and two neighbours for every other hole.
  • The lists of what a closure must contain were not exhaustive, since further neighbours also witness collisions. They were completed, and the calibration's bound was re-derived with \(2p\) further neighbours per hole.
  • "Per unit of rank" and a comparison with the Lemma were overclaims and were removed.
  • The rejection argument needed \(0/1\) solutions and implication over \(0/1\) points. It did not use rank one, and it needs the Delayer step only below rank \(m\).
  • The extendability notion needed the row condition, and it is now marked as a proposal. Freedom alone does not make the example inconsistent.

These fixes weaken or qualify claims. The one extension, to every prime, is the reviewer's own check, so no second pass was run. No computation was run.

A vertex-cover closure for plain unary PHP over \(\mathbb F_p\): size, leaves and span weakening hold, but hole covers trap pigeons and the Delayer step fails through the greedy continuation

22 September 2026 · Working proofs of size, leaves, span weakening and an onto lemma; a counterexample to the Delayer reduction. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The forced-cell test showed that local consistency for unary PHP over \(\mathbb F_p\) cannot be defined by forcing. It proposed a closure defined by extendability and asked for a size bound \(C_p\cdot\text{rank}\), or a rank-one family whose closure grows with \(n\). This entry defines a closure that does not depend on right-hand sides and proves its size bound, the leaf property and weakening under span containment. The third property Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson's path argument needs is the Delayer step. The entry's first reduction of it was refuted in review by a trapped-pigeon example, recorded below. The entry also finds a rank-one family of the kind asked for, but only for functional PHP. The test ends with the closure's properties proved or refuted, and the open part stated exactly.

Setting and definitions

Let \(G\) be a bipartite graph between pigeons and holes, with cells \(x_{ih}\in\{0,1\}\). The target is plain PHP on \(G\): pigeon clauses \(\bigvee_{h\in N(i)}x_{ih}\) and hole clauses \(\neg x_{ih}\vee\neg x_{jh}\), with no functional clauses. This is the thread's default weak PHP. Linear forms are over \(\mathbb F_p\). For a set \(S\) of rows and holes, \(F[\backslash S]\) sets to zero every cell in a row or a hole of \(S\). For a set \(X\) of cells, \(\tau(X)\) is the least number of rows and holes covering \(X\), which by König's theorem is its matching number.

  • Danger. Fix \(\theta\ge1\). A nonzero subspace \(U\) of forms is \(\theta\)-dangerous when \(\tau(\operatorname{supp}U)<\theta\dim U\). A set \(F\) is \(\theta\)-safe when \(\langle F\rangle\) has no \(\theta\)-dangerous subspace. The notion depends on the forms only, not on right-hand sides.
  • Greedy closure. Starting from a set \(S_0\), while \(\langle F[\backslash S]\rangle\) has a \(\theta\)-dangerous subspace \(U\), add to \(S\) a minimum cover of \(\operatorname{supp}U\).
  • Injective solutions. A \(0/1\) assignment is \(S\)-injective when every hole of \(S\) holds at most one pigeon, and every pigeon of \(S\) lies in at least one hole, in holes that no other pigeon of \(S\) uses. Every pigeon whose holes all lie in \(S\) counts as a pigeon of \(S\).
  • Local consistency. Fix a budget \(B\). A system \(\Phi\) is locally consistent when some \(S\) with \(|S|\le B\) makes \(\Phi[\backslash S]\) \(\theta\)-safe and \(\Phi\) has an \(S\)-injective \(0/1\) solution. The occupancy equations are left out here; see the open list below.

Size

Lemma A (potential). Every step of the greedy closure strictly decreases \(|S|+\theta\dim\langle F[\backslash S]\rangle\). So the output \(S\) satisfies \(|S|\le|S_0|+\theta\dim\langle F[\backslash S_0]\rangle\), and from \(S_0=\varnothing\), \(|S|\le\theta\operatorname{rank}F\).

Proof. Let \(U\) be the dangerous subspace, of dimension \(d\), and \(K\) its cover, with \(|K|=\tau(\operatorname{supp}U)<\theta d\). Zeroing \(K\) is a linear map from \(\langle F[\backslash S]\rangle\) onto \(\langle F[\backslash(S\cup K)]\rangle\), and it kills \(U\), since every form in \(U\) is supported on cells that \(K\) covers. So the dimension drops by at least \(d\), while \(|S|\) grows by less than \(\theta d\). \(\square\)

Adding one form raises \(\dim\langle F[\backslash S]\rangle\) by at most one, so the potential rises by at most \(\theta\) per added form. The closure therefore stays within \(\theta\) times the number of added forms.

Leaves, weakening, and the examples

Proposition B.

  1. Weakening under span containment. If \(\Phi\) is locally consistent with witness \(S\), and \(\Psi\) is implied by \(\Phi\) over \(0/1\) points with \(\langle\Psi\rangle\subseteq\langle\Phi\rangle\), then \(\Psi\) is locally consistent with the same \(S\). Every subspace of \(\langle\Psi[\backslash S]\rangle\) lies in \(\langle\Phi[\backslash S]\rangle\), and an \(S\)-injective solution of \(\Phi\) solves \(\Psi\). The span hypothesis matters. Over \(\mathbb F_2\), Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson derive it from semantic implication, but over \(\mathbb F_p\) with \(0/1\) points it does not follow: over \(\mathbb F_3\), \(x_1+x_2=2\) implies \(x_1=1\). So the path argument over \(\mathbb F_p\) must use proof rules whose premises' forms lie in the span of the conclusion's negation and the resolved form.
  2. Leaves. Let \(\theta>1\). The negation of a hole clause, \(\{x_{ih}=1,\ x_{jh}=1\}\), is not locally consistent. Each single-cell form has cover number \(1<\theta\), so a witness must cover cell \(ih\) by row \(i\) or hole \(h\), and likewise \(jh\). Then it contains \(h\), which would hold two pigeons, or both \(i\) and \(j\), which would share \(h\). The negation of a pigeon clause, \(\{x_{ih}=0:h\in N(i)\}\), is not locally consistent either. A witness contains row \(i\), or all of \(N(i)\), and then \(i\) counts as a pigeon of \(S\). Either way \(i\) must lie in a hole. The empty system is locally consistent, with witness \(\varnothing\), if no pigeon is isolated.
  3. The examples. Let \(\theta>p-2\). The form \(x_{1a}+x_{2a}+x_{3a}\) of the forced-cell test has cover number \(1\). Any witness contains \(a\), or rows \(1,2,3\). So the equation \(=2\) is not locally consistent, while \(=0\) and \(=1\) are with witness \(\{a\}\), provided pigeons \(1,2,3\) have holes other than \(a\); otherwise \(\{a\}\) traps them. The calibration form, over \(k\le p-2\) holes with two pigeons each, has cover number \(k<\theta\). A witness therefore covers every one of its cells, and an \(S\)-injective solution has at most one pigeon per hole, so the value \(k+1\) is rejected. Both results match the necessary condition recorded there.

The free part is realizable

Lemma C (onto). Let \(F\) be a set of forms over \(\mathbb F_p\) in \(0/1\) variables, of rank \(r\ge1\). Let \(l\) be an integer with \((1-1/p)^{\,l-p+2}\,r<1\); \(l\ge p\ln r+p-1\) suffices. Suppose \(|\operatorname{supp}U|\ge l\dim U\) for every nonzero subspace \(U\subseteq\langle F\rangle\). Then every value of \(F\) attained by some assignment over \(\mathbb F_p\) is attained by a \(0/1\) assignment.

Proof. Choose independent \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\) spanning \(\langle F\rangle\) and let \(c_t\in\mathbb F_p^r\) be the column of variable \(t\). The columns span \(\mathbb F_p^r\), and it suffices to attain every value of \(g\). For a set \(A\) of variables whose columns span \(W\), the forms vanishing on \(W\) make up a subspace \(U\) of dimension \(r-\dim W\), and \(\operatorname{supp}U\) is the set of variables with column outside \(W\). So the hypothesis says that at least \(l(r-\operatorname{rank}A)\) variables lie outside every such \(A\). By the Nash-Williams–Edmonds base-packing theorem, the columns contain \(l\) disjoint bases. By Alon, Linial and Meshulam's Proposition 3.1, the union of \(l\) bases of \(\mathbb F_p^r\) with \((1-1/p)^{l-p+2}r<1\) is an additive basis. Every vector is then a sum of a subset of the columns, which is the value at a \(0/1\) assignment. The sufficient bound follows from \((1-1/p)^{p\ln r+1}r<e^{-\ln r}r=1\). \(\square\)

A \(\theta\)-safe set with \(\theta\ge l\) satisfies the hypothesis, since \(|\operatorname{supp}U|\ge\tau(\operatorname{supp}U)\). For \(r=1\) the lemma is Cauchy–Davenport: \(p-1\) nonzero coefficients reach every value.

The Delayer step: a first reduction and its failure

Suppose \(\Phi\) is locally consistent with witness \(S\) and \(S\)-injective solution \(x\), and let \(f\) be a form. The first reduction continues the greedy closure on \((\Phi\cup\{f\})[\backslash S]\) to \(S'=S\cup N\). If \(|S'|\le B\) and \(\Phi\) has an \(S'\)-injective solution \(y\), then \(\alpha=f(y)\) keeps \(\Phi\wedge(f=\alpha)\) locally consistent with witness \(S'\). To build \(y\), keep \(x\) on the cells of \(S\) and choose the cells of \(N\). The free cells then have to realize the remaining values of \(\Phi[\backslash S']\), a subspace of the safe \((\Phi\cup\{f\})[\backslash S']\). By Lemma C they can, provided \(\theta\ge l\) for its rank; \(\theta\ge p\ln|\text{cells}|+p-1\) suffices for all ranks. The values are consistent exactly when \(\psi(y_N)=\psi(x)\) for every form \(\psi\) of \(\langle\Phi[\backslash S]\rangle\) supported on the cells of \(N\), where \(y_N\) is the assignment on those cells. So only the value that \(x\) gives is needed. Two conditions remain: the budget \(|S'|\le B\), which fails along a path when witnesses are carried, and an \(N\)-injective \(y_N\) with those values.

Counterexample, found in review. The second condition can fail even when no form is supported on \(N\). Take \[ \Phi=\{x_{as_1}+x_{cs_1}=1,\ x_{bs_2}+x_{ds_2}=1\}. \] Each form has cover number \(1\), with the unique minimum covers \(\{s_1\}\) and \(\{s_2\}\), so the greedy closure is \(S=\{s_1,s_2\}\). Let \(x\) put \(a\) in \(s_1\) and \(b\) in \(s_2\). Now let \(f=x_{kh}+x_{k'h}\), with \(N(k)=\{s_1,h\}\) and \(N(k')=\{s_2,h\}\). Its unique minimum cover is \(\{h\}\), so \(N=\{h\}\). Then \(k\) and \(k'\) are trapped. Each must lie in a hole. By \(\Phi\), \(s_1\) holds one of \(a,c\) and \(s_2\) one of \(b,d\), and a hole of \(S\) holds at most one pigeon, so both must use \(h\). So \(\Phi\) has no \(S'\)-injective solution at all, for any \(x\) and any \(\alpha\). Yet, if \(c\) has a hole other than \(s_1\), \(\Phi\wedge(f=1)\) is locally consistent with the different witness \(\{a,c,s_2,h\}\): put \(a\) in \(s_1\), \(c\) in another hole, \(b\) in \(s_2\), \(k'\) in \(h\) and \(k\) in \(s_1\). This works for every \(\theta>1\) and every \(p\). So the reduction through the greedy continuation is refuted.

The failure is Hall's condition for the pigeons the closure places, not linear algebra. Hole covers make it worse because they trap pigeons, but covers by rows alone fail on the same example: \(k\) and \(k'\) would join the closure and still have only \(h\) free. Two changes are needed.

  • A graph with expansion. The standard remedy for graph PHP is a bipartite expander and a budget small against its expansion. Then every small set of pigeons keeps many free holes after the closure's holes and pigeons are removed.
  • A cover-choice rule. Covers should be chosen by a rule that keeps Hall's condition, or by the Delayer, not by the greedy minimum.

(MR′), open. On such an expander, with such a rule, let \(G_N\) be the forms of \(\langle\Phi[\backslash S]\rangle\) supported on the cells of the new part \(N\). The question is whether some assignment to those cells takes the values that \(x\) gives on \(G_N\), is injective on \(N\) and its trapped pigeons, and is compatible with \(x\) on \(S\). For \(\dim G_N=1\) a natural route uses a matching of at least \(p-1\) cells in the support, which exists by König's theorem, and switches along it. For larger dimension a natural route is a matching whose columns contain an additive basis. That is a common independent set of the \(l\)-fold union of the column matroid and two partition matroids. No general min-max theorem is known for such intersections, and the problem is NP-hard in general. A greedy matching is guaranteed at least a fraction \(\theta/(\theta+2)\) of the rank: it stops at size \(s\) with the uncovered forms supported on the \(2s\) rows and holes it used. A topological Hall theorem, Aharoni and Berger's for a matroid and a simplicial complex, is a lead: it would need a lower bound on the connectivity of bipartite matching complexes, which was not checked here.

Size. Lemma C needs \(\theta\ge l\approx p\ln r+p-1\), so the closure bound \(\theta\cdot\text{rank}\) is \(O(p\,r\log r)\), not \(C_p\cdot\text{rank}\) for a constant \(C_p\). A constant \(\theta\) would need the conjecture of Jaeger, Linial, Payan and Tarsi that a number of bases depending on \(p\) alone forms an additive basis, which Alon, Linial and Meshulam record as open.

Two limits found on the way

  • No canonical closure. For \(F=\{x_{1a}+\cdots+x_{ma}\}\) and \(\theta>1\), the sets \(S\) that make \(F[\backslash S]\) safe are those containing \(a\) or all rows \(1,\ldots,m\). The two minimal ones, \(\{a\}\) and \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\), meet in the empty set, which is not closing, and their union has \(m+1\) elements. So there is no least closing set, and the union of the minimal ones is not bounded by the rank. Local consistency above therefore uses an existential witness. That suffices for the weakening step, but Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson's rank argument also compares the closures of a clause and its premises. With witnesses carried along a path, the size bound is in the number of steps, not in the rank. Arguments that recompute a closure at each node, as the random walk with restarts does, can use Lemma A there. They then need a solution injective on the recomputed closure, which the walk has to supply.
  • Functional PHP needs row sums exempted. With functional clauses \(\neg x_{ih}\vee\neg x_{ih'}\), a pigeon of \(S\) must lie in exactly one hole. The rank-one system \(\sum_{i\in R}\sum_{h}x_{ih}=|R|+1\) then forces a violation among \(R\) in every \(0/1\) solution. By the rejection argument of the forced-cell test, it must be locally inconsistent when the Delayer step holds up to rank \(\sum_{i\in R}\deg i\). A solution can place the violation at any pigeon of \(R\) with degree at least two, so a closure that sees it covers all cells of \(R\). Its size is at least their cover number, which is \(|R|\) when \(R\) has a matching into its holes. One equation then needs a closure unbounded in the rank. For plain PHP a pigeon may lie in several holes, and the system is harmless. For functional PHP, the row sums would have to be exempted, as the column sums are, which runs into the safety cap of the column dichotomy.

Assessment

The closure sub-line now has a definition with a proved size bound, of order \(p\,r\log r\), the leaf property, weakening under span containment, and an onto lemma for the free part without the occupancy equations. The Delayer step is open and its first reduction is refuted. The refutation is a Hall failure that an expander and a cover-choice rule should address, but that is a further design step, not a repair. Four items remain open, in order of risk:

  1. the Delayer step on expanders, with (MR′);
  2. the occupancy equations, which a single hole's cover number already flags as dangerous;
  3. a canonical closure, or a path argument that recomputes closures;
  4. F_p proof rules with span containment for weakening.

Beyond these, the bounded-depth route still needs the probability bound, a restriction step and search hardness, and its payoff is a bounded-depth endpoint, not the goal. The sub-line's prospects remain weak.

Sheaf check

The closure is where local sections are pinned down: pigeons and holes whose placement the system constrains. Outside it, Lemma C says every section extends, as long as the forms spread over enough cells. The counterexample is a gluing failure of a different kind: pinning a hole removes it from every neighbouring pigeon's options, so sections on the closure can fail to extend for reasons of matching alone. Expansion is the condition under which removing a few holes and pigeons leaves the matching sheaf flabby.

Next step

Next step (odd-prime-clause-transfer): restate local consistency on a bipartite expander with a cover-choice rule that preserves Hall's condition. Then prove the Delayer step in its smallest cases. In dimension \(0\) the question is Hall's condition alone, and in dimension \(1\) it is one form with \(p-1\) switches along a matching. Exhaustive search is not an option beyond dimension one. At \(p=3\), dimension two and \(\theta=3\), a cover number of at least \(6\) needs a six-cell matching, so at least six rows and six holes. The two-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb F_3^{36}\) number about \(3^{68}\). If the small cases hold, read Aharoni and Berger's theorem and the connectivity of bipartite matching complexes for the general case.

Verification gate. Re-read verbatim: Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson's Sections 1.3.3 and 4, and Alon, Linial and Meshulam's Proposition 3.1 in the source. The Nash-Williams–Edmonds base-packing theorem is standard and imported. Aharoni and Berger's theorem was read only in a search summary and is not used. Record searches for base packing, additive bases, vertex-cover closures and potentials, and row-count obstructions found nothing that implies Lemmas A and C or the closure. The nearest records, the forced-cell lemma and a row-transversal criterion, are different statements. Before review, I corrected four points in my own draft: an unused degree hypothesis, the rank-one case of (MR) stated as proved, an overclaim about recomputed closures, and the test size. A fresh-context reviewer then checked the entry. Verdict: gap. Lemmas A and C, the leaves and span weakening check out. The reviewer refuted the draft's reduction of the Delayer step with the trapped-pigeon example, which I verified and recorded above. The reduction and "(MR)" were withdrawn, and the title and assessment were revised. The reviewer also required these fixes:

  • the span hypothesis for weakening, which semantic implication over \(\mathbb F_p\) does not give;
  • the size \(O(p\,r\log r)\) in place of \(C_p\cdot\text{rank}\);
  • the consistency condition \(\psi(y_N)=\psi(x)\), and the budget as a separate condition;
  • the greedy fraction as a guarantee;
  • the union matroid in the matroid remark;
  • the proviso on pigeons \(1,2,3\) in the example;
  • the cover-number wording in the functional bullet;
  • local consistency of the empty system;
  • a next step that starts in dimensions \(0\) and \(1\), with the count for dimension two made now.

These fixes remove or weaken claims. The one added claim is the reviewer's own counterexample, which I checked. So no second pass was run. No computation was run.

Route review: the vertex-cover closure handles rank-one collisions, but block column sums revive the column dichotomy and the Delayer step is open; the closure sub-line stays weak

22 September 2026 · Route review of the closure sub-line · Weak; block column sums revive the column dichotomy; next: danger modulo the occupancy span, then Hall on expanders. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

The line's general claim. A closure theory for unary PHP over \(\mathbb F_p\) would support Efremenko, Garlík and Itsykson's path argument and, with a hard distribution, Byramji and Impagliazzo's random walk. It would give size lower bounds for \(\mathrm{Res}(\mathrm{lin}_{\mathbb F_p})\) refutations of bounded depth. What the goal needs is more: the thread's goal is unrestricted refutations, and bounded depth is a restriction. The line is the only recorded candidate that could handle more than \(Cn\) window lines, if it can be built. Since the last route review, two cycles have tested closure candidates. The forced-cell test refuted forcing as a basis for local consistency. The vertex-cover closure proved a size bound, the leaf property and weakening under span containment, and its reviewer refuted the greedy reduction of its Delayer step.

Falsification attempt: the live candidate against the recorded obstructions

The candidate is the vertex-cover closure: a subspace \(U\) of forms is dangerous when the rows and holes covering its support number fewer than \(\theta\dim U\). The candidate was checked against each obstruction recorded on this line.

  1. Rank-one collisions. \(x_{1a}+x_{2a}+x_{3a}=2\) forces a collision at rank one. Its support has cover number one, so it is dangerous, and the value \(2\) is rejected. So is the calibration family. Handled.
  2. The column dichotomy. Every nonzero form on a single hole is dangerous. So is every system of occupancy forms with fewer than \(\theta\) holes per dimension: \(r\) occupancy forms on distinct holes have cover number at most \(r<\theta r\). But block sums behave differently. Take disjoint blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_r\) of \(\theta\) holes each, with a single matching covering their union. The system of sums \(\sum_{h\in B_j}\mathrm{col}_h\) is \(\theta\)-safe. These sums have disjoint supports, so a subspace \(U\) is supported on all cells at the holes of \(\bigcup_{j\in J}B_j\), for some \(J\) with \(|J|\ge\dim U\). By König's theorem that support has cover number \(\theta|J|\ge\theta\dim U\). One matching for each block separately is not enough: two blocks whose holes meet only the same \(\theta\) pigeons have cover number \(\theta<2\theta\). The dichotomy's proof applies to block sums, as checked below. A block whose sum differs from its size contains a visible hole, whose occupancy is not \(1\) modulo \(p\). So, if safe block systems are charged, a linear tree of depth \(O(r_0\theta\log(2/\eta)(\log n+\log(2/\eta)))\) finds a falsified hole clause with high probability. For fixed \(\eta\) and a charge \(2^{-cr_0}\), the depth is \(O(\theta\log n)\). So, for the random walk's probability bound, the obstruction survives under the vertex-cover notion, with its depth threshold raised by the factor \(\theta\). A constant \(\theta\) would need the open additive-basis conjecture of item 6. The alternative is a danger notion that does not charge safe block systems. Measuring danger modulo the occupancy span is one candidate way to do that, and it belongs to the open item on the occupancy equations. For the distribution-free path argument the obstruction does not arise.
  3. The safety cap. The cap concerned safety with pigeon rows as blocks. A witness can pin the holes of the occupancy forms that actually appear in a system, at a cost of one per hole. But the occupancy equations themselves were left out of local consistency and remain open.
  4. Functional PHP. For functional PHP, one row-count equation over pigeons \(R\) needs a closure at least the cover number of \(R\)'s cells, which is \(|R|\) when \(R\) has a matching into its holes. This holds if the Delayer step holds up to rank \(\sum_{i\in R}\deg i\). So the candidate is restricted to plain PHP, the thread's default. A lower bound for plain PHP is the weaker statement.
  5. No canonical closure, and weakening. No least closing set exists, so local consistency uses an existential witness. A path argument then bounds the closure by the number of steps, not the rank. Weakening holds under span containment, which semantic implication over \(\mathbb F_p\) with \(0/1\) points does not give. So the path argument needs proof rules with that property. Open.
  6. Size. The onto lemma needs \(\theta\) of order \(p\ln r\), so the closure bound is \(O(p\,r\log r)\). A constant \(\theta\) would need the open conjecture of Jaeger, Linial, Payan and Tarsi. Accepted for bounded depth.
  7. The Delayer step. Its reduction through the greedy continuation is refuted by the trapped-pigeon example. Covers by rows fail on the same example, because the pigeons that join the closure still have only one free hole. What is refuted is the reduction, not the Delayer step. The step also needs (MR′): an assignment on the new cells, injective there, with prescribed values. The natural route is a matching whose columns contain an additive basis, a matroid intersection with no known min-max theorem that is NP-hard in general. Open.

Block sums, checked here. Let \(\theta\ge1\) be an integer with \(r_0\theta\le n_0\). In the column dichotomy's step 1, replace the random set \(H'\) of \(r_0\) holes by \(r_0\) disjoint blocks of \(\theta\) holes of \(H_0\), chosen uniformly at random, so that each chosen hole is uniform on \(H_0\). The hypothesis is that, over the blocks and \(\nu\) together, every chosen block sum is \(\theta\) modulo \(p\) with probability at most \(\delta\). A fixed assignment with \(|V\cap H_0|\le n_0/(4r_0\theta)\) has all chosen blocks disjoint from the visible set \(V\) with probability at least \(3/4\), by the union bound over the \(r_0\theta\) chosen holes. Then every chosen block sum equals the block size modulo \(p\). So the hypothesis gives \(\nu(|V\cap H_0|\le n_0/(4r_0\theta))\le\tfrac43\delta\). Steps 2 to 4 run as before with \(r_0\theta\) in place of \(r_0\). The success probability of one trial becomes at least \(1/(34r_0\theta)\), which gives the stated depth.

Assessment

  • odd-prime-clause-transfer, the window: weak, unchanged.
  • odd-prime-clause-transfer, the closure sub-line: weak. The vertex-cover closure handles rank-one collisions and has a size bound, the leaf property and span weakening. Four items are open, in order of risk:
    1. the occupancy span: block sums revive the column dichotomy for the random walk, so either its depth threshold rises by the factor \(\theta\), or the danger notion must stop charging safe block systems, for instance by measuring danger modulo the occupancy span;
    2. the Delayer step, with Hall's condition for the closure's own pigeons and (MR′);
    3. proof rules with span containment;
    4. a canonical closure, or a path argument that recomputes closures.
    Expanders and a Hall-preserving cover rule are a further design step, not a known repair. After these come the probability bound, the restriction step and search hardness. The payoff is still limited to bounded depth.
  • same-graph-composition: nothing open.
  • scope-and-review: complete up to external review. The write-up and the binary compiler audit await user decisions.

Next step

Next step (odd-prime-clause-transfer): test the candidate remedy for block sums first, because for the random walk they are where the dichotomy bites. Define danger modulo the occupancy span, measuring each subspace by the cover number of its best representative modulo that span. Test whether Lemma A's potential bound and the leaf property survive. Then extend the onto lemma to the occupancy equations. After that, restate the closure on a bounded-degree expander. Require Hall's condition for the closure's own pigeons into the holes that are not pinned. The test case is the trapped-pigeon example's analogue on an expander: a pigeon of degree \(d\) whose other \(d-1\) holes the closure pins.

Sheaf check

The vertex-cover notion pins a hole's occupancy as a local section when it appears alone. Summed over enough holes, occupancy becomes a safe, global-looking section again, and the column dichotomy returns. Quotienting the occupancy span out, instead of pinning it piece by piece, is the candidate remedy. Hall's condition for the pinned pigeons, and the injective gluing (MR′) on new closure cells, remain the other two gluing obstructions.

Verification gate. No result is registered. Re-read in full: the vertex-cover closure entry, the forced-cell test, and the proposition and proof of the column dichotomy, whose proof the block-sum paragraph adapts. Two fresh-context review passes were run.

  • First pass. Verdict: sound with fixes. It showed that the draft's claim that the column dichotomy does not apply was false, because block column sums over at least \(\theta\) holes are safe. It also found that several items strengthened the previous entry, and that the draft omitted two of its limits: span containment and the size \(O(p\,r\log r)\). Further fixes: the assessment and sheaf check overclaimed, and the next step's test case was vacuous. The entry was rewritten. The rewrite added the block-sum extension of the dichotomy.
  • Second pass. It checked the extension, which adds a claim. Verdict: sound with fixes. Safety needs one matching over all blocks. The random-block hypotheses had to be stated. The obstruction survives with its depth threshold raised by the factor \(\theta\). Quotienting by the occupancy span is a candidate remedy, not a forced one. These fixes only qualify claims.

No computation was run.

The vertex-cover closure modulo the occupancy span: occupancy forms are exempted without a cap, the potential bound and the leaves survive, and the onto lemma extends to the occupancy equations

22 September 2026 · Working proofs for plain unary PHP over \(\mathbb F_p\): potential, leaves, block sums and the onto lemma, modulo the occupancy span. The Delayer step remains open. Produced by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5, high effort).

Question. Route item: odd-prime-clause-transfer. The route review found that block column sums over at least \(\theta\) holes are safe under the vertex-cover closure. It found that the column dichotomy then applies to them, with its depth threshold raised by the factor \(\theta\). It proposed measuring danger modulo the occupancy span, and testing whether the potential bound and the leaf property survive, and whether the onto lemma extends to the occupancy equations. The test ends when each of these holds or fails.

Definitions

Let \(G\) be a bipartite graph between pigeons and holes in which every hole has at least two neighbours. The target is plain PHP on \(G\). Forms are over \(\mathbb F_p\) in the cells \(x_{ih}\in\{0,1\}\), and \(O\) is the occupancy equations \(\mathrm{col}_h=1\), \(h\in H\). For a set \(S\) of rows and holes, \(W_S=\langle\mathrm{col}_h[\backslash S]:h\notin S\rangle\) is the occupancy span after \(S\) is zeroed.

  • Danger modulo \(W\). For a subspace \(U\subseteq\langle F[\backslash S]\rangle\), let \(d_W(U)=\dim\bigl((U+W_S)/W_S\bigr)\). Let \(\tau_W(U)\) be the least cover number \(\tau(\operatorname{supp}U')\) over subspaces \(U'\) with \(U'+W_S=U+W_S\) and \(\dim U'=d_W(U)\), the representatives of \(U\). \(U\) is \(\theta\)-dangerous modulo \(W\) when \(d_W(U)\ge1\) and \(\tau_W(U)<\theta\,d_W(U)\), and \(F[\backslash S]\) is safe modulo \(W\) when no subspace is.
  • Greedy closure. While \(\langle F[\backslash S]\rangle\) has a dangerous subspace \(U\), take a representative \(U'\) with \(\tau(\operatorname{supp}U')=\tau_W(U)\), and add a minimum cover of \(\operatorname{supp}U'\) to \(S\).
  • Absorbed cells and pigeons of \(S\). A cell \(ih\) with \(i\) and \(h\) outside \(S\) is absorbed when every other cell of column \(h\) lies in a row of \(S\). Then \(\mathrm{col}_h[\backslash S]=x_{ih}\), and \(O\) determines \(x_{ih}\) from the cells of \(S\). A pigeon counts as a pigeon of \(S\) when each of its cells is zeroed by \(S\) or absorbed. This extends the earlier rule for pigeons whose holes all lie in \(S\).
  • Local consistency. Fix a budget \(\beta\). \(\Phi\) is locally consistent when some \(S\) with \(|S|\le\beta\) makes \(\Phi[\backslash S]\) safe modulo \(W\), and \(\Phi\cup O\) has an \(S\)-injective \(0/1\) solution. That is, every hole of \(S\) holds at most one pigeon, and every pigeon of \(S\) lies in at least one hole, in holes no other pigeon of \(S\) uses.

The potential bound

Lemma A\(_W\). Every step of the greedy closure strictly decreases \(|S|+\theta\dim\bigl((\langle F[\backslash S]\rangle+W_S)/W_S\bigr)\). So from \(S_0=\varnothing\), \(|S|\le\theta\dim\bigl((\langle F\rangle+W)/W\bigr)\).

Proof. Zeroing the cover \(K\) maps \(\langle F[\backslash S]\rangle+W_S\) onto \(\langle F[\backslash(S\cup K)]\rangle+W_{S\cup K}\), and it maps \(W_S\) onto \(W_{S\cup K}\), since \(\mathrm{col}_h[\backslash S]\) goes to \(\mathrm{col}_h[\backslash(S\cup K)]\), which is zero for \(h\in K\). So it induces a surjection of the quotients by the occupancy spans. The representative \(U'\) lies in \(\langle F[\backslash S]\rangle+W_S\), meets \(W_S\) only in \(0\), and has dimension \(d=d_W(U)\). Its image in the first quotient therefore has dimension \(d\), and it lies in the kernel, since \(K\) covers \(\operatorname{supp}U'\). So the quotient dimension drops by at least \(d\), while \(|S|\) grows by \(\tau_W(U)<\theta d\). \(\square\)

Block sums \(\sum_{h\in B}\mathrm{col}_h\), and every other form of the occupancy span, have \(d_W=0\), so they are exempted, as Byramji and Impagliazzo exempt column sums. The column dichotomy said exemption fails for fixed \(p\). The reason was the safety cap: with pigeon rows as blocks, a safe system has room for at most \(p\) forms beside the occupancy span. Here danger is measured by covers of representatives modulo the span, not by counting forms against rows, so no cap arises. The exempted values are fixed by \(O\), which local consistency imposes, and any other value of a block sum contradicts \(O\). So the column dichotomy's charged horn does not arise, because block sums are not charged, and its exempted horn is no longer blocked by the cap. Whether the probability bound holds for the remaining safe systems is a separate question.

Leaves and the examples

Proposition B\(_W\). Let \(\theta>1\). The empty system is locally consistent with witness \(\varnothing\): since every hole has at least two neighbours, no cell is absorbed and no pigeon counts as a pigeon of \(\varnothing\), and \(O\) has a \(0/1\) solution, one cell per column.

  1. Hole clauses. \(\{x_{ih}=1,\ x_{jh}=1\}\) is not locally consistent. A single cell \(x_{ih}\) is its own representative, supported in column \(h\), so its \(\tau_W\) is at most \(1\). A witness must therefore make it zero or put it into \(W_S\). The only element of \(W_S\) that can equal \(x_{ih}\) is \(\mathrm{col}_h[\backslash S]\). So the witness kills the cell by row \(i\), by hole \(h\), or by absorbing \(ih\), which puts every other neighbour of \(h\) into \(S\). The same holds for \(jh\). If \(h\in S\), then \(h\) holds two pigeons. If \(i,j\in S\), they share \(h\). Otherwise exactly one of \(i,j\) is in \(S\), and the other's cell is absorbed. Then two pigeons lie in \(h\), and all neighbours of \(h\) except the one outside \(S\) are in \(S\). By \(O\) the occupancy of \(h\) is then at least \(p+1\), so at least \(p-1\ge1\) further pigeons of \(S\) lie in \(h\), next to the one of \(i,j\) in \(S\). Two pigeons of \(S\) share a hole.
  2. Pigeon clauses. \(\{x_{ih}=0:h\in N(i)\}\) is not locally consistent. A witness kills every cell of \(i\), by row \(i\), by its hole, or by absorbing it. Then \(i\) counts as a pigeon of \(S\) and must lie in a hole.
  3. The examples. \(x_{1a}+x_{2a}+x_{3a}\) is its own representative, supported in column \(a\), so it is dangerous unless the witness makes it zero or puts it into \(W_S\). The witness pins \(a\), or takes rows \(1,2,3\), or takes every neighbour of \(a\) outside \(\{1,2,3\}\), possibly with some of \(1,2,3\). In the last case, with the value \(2\), two of the pigeons \(1,2,3\) lie in \(a\). By \(O\) the occupancy of \(a\) is then at least \(p+1\), so at least \(p-1\ge2\) further pigeons lie in \(a\), all of them in \(S\). So the value \(2\) is rejected in every case, as the rejection argument requires. The calibration family, over \(k\le p-2\) holes, is rejected in the same way when \(\theta>p-2\). For \(\theta\le k\) its form can be safe with \(S=\varnothing\), and then a solution with one hole holding \(p+1\) pigeons outside \(S\) accepts the value \(k+1\).

The onto lemma with the occupancy equations

Lemma C\(_W\). Let \(l\) be as in Lemma C for rank \(r\), the rank of \(\Phi\cup O\). Suppose \(\Phi\) is safe modulo \(W\) with \(\theta\ge2l\), and every hole has at least \(2l\) cells. Then every value of \(\Phi\cup O\) attained over \(\mathbb F_p\) is attained by a \(0/1\) assignment.

Proof. Lemma C needs \(|\operatorname{supp}U|\ge l\dim U\) for every nonzero \(U\subseteq\langle\Phi\cup O\rangle\). The number \(\tau_W(U)\) depends only on \(U+W\). For \(U\subseteq\langle\Phi\rangle+W\), the modular law gives \(U+W=V+W\) with \(V=(U+W)\cap\langle\Phi\rangle\), so safety of \(\Phi\) modulo \(W\) bounds it for every such \(U\). Let \(d_1=\dim(U\cap W)\) and \(d_2=\dim U-d_1\), and let \(U''\subseteq U\) be a complement of \(U\cap W\). A subspace of \(W\) of dimension \(d_1\) contains, for each of at least \(d_1\) holes, an element in which that column has a nonzero coefficient. Its support therefore covers those columns in full, which is at least \(2l\,d_1\) cells. \(U''\) is a representative of \(U\) modulo \(W\). If \(d_2\ge1\), safety gives \(|\operatorname{supp}U''|\ge\tau(\operatorname{supp}U'')\ge\theta d_2\ge2l\,d_2\). Both supports lie in \(\operatorname{supp}U\), so \(|\operatorname{supp}U|\ge\max(2ld_1,2ld_2)\ge l(d_1+d_2)\). \(\square\)

In the Delayer step the lemma is applied to the free cells, so every hole outside the closure needs \(2l\) free cells. With \(l\) of order \(p\ln r\), the graph needs degree at least of order \(p\log n\). That is necessary, not sufficient: the closure does not by itself keep \(2l\) free cells in every column, since an absorbed hole has one free cell and closure rows erode columns. The free-cell condition is part of what the expander step must provide. A graph restriction of that degree still transfers lower bounds to full PHP.

What remains

  • The Delayer step. Its greedy reduction was refuted by trapped pigeons, and absorbed cells now trap pigeons too. The next obligation is Hall's condition for the closure's own pigeons on an expander, and then (MR′).
  • Row sums, an open question. The random walk's hard distribution is functional, and row sums are fixed for the pigeons it maps. Whether the probability bound also needs a quotient by row sums is open. Two cautions apply. First, \(\sum_i\mathrm{row}_i=\sum_h\mathrm{col}_h\), so modulo \(W\) a row sum over a set of pigeons is minus the row sum over the complement, and its danger depends on both. Second, imposing every row equation together with \(O\) is inconsistent over \(\mathbb F_p\) when the numbers of pigeons and holes differ modulo \(p\). A distribution with occupancy one per hole also leaves some pigeons unmapped. Any row quotient would have to impose only some row equations.
  • Span containment, a canonical closure, the probability bound, the restriction step and search hardness, as recorded in the route review.

Assessment

The candidate remedy works where it was tested. The quotient keeps the potential bound and the leaves, and exempts block column sums without the safety cap. It also makes the free part realizable together with the occupancy equations, provided every hole outside the closure keeps at least \(2l\) free cells, which needs degree at least of order \(p\log n\). Row sums under a functional distribution are an open question on the other side. The Delayer step is still the main open item. The closure sub-line is still weak: several design steps remain, and the payoff is limited to bounded depth.

Sheaf check

Quotienting by the occupancy span treats hole occupancy as data fixed by the distribution, as Byramji and Impagliazzo treat their column sums. The difference from the safety cap is that danger is measured by covers of representatives, not by counting forms against rows. So the quotient costs nothing in the bound. Absorbed cells are the local shadow of the quotient: a cell whose column is otherwise pinned is determined by the global section. Its pigeon joins the closure when all of the pigeon's cells are zeroed or absorbed.

Next step

Next step (odd-prime-clause-transfer): the Delayer step on an expander of degree of order \(p\log n\), modulo the occupancy span. Add to the closure the pigeons whose free neighbourhood becomes too small, and prove Hall's condition for the closure's own pigeons into the holes that are not pinned. The test case is a pigeon of degree \(d\) whose other \(d-1\) holes are pinned or absorbed. In parallel, decide which row equations a functional hard distribution would let local consistency impose.

Verification gate. Re-read in full: the vertex-cover closure (Lemmas A and C, the leaves), the route review (block sums) and the column dichotomy (the safety cap). Record searches for danger modulo the occupancy span, absorbed cells and trapped pigeons, and onto lemmas with occupancy found nothing that implies these statements. Before review, I corrected three points in my own draft: which representatives a single cell has, the mixed witnesses in the example, and why safety covers subspaces of \(\langle\Phi\rangle+W\). A fresh-context reviewer checked the entry. Verdict: sound with fixes. It confirmed Lemma A\(_W\), the hole and pigeon leaves under \(O\), the three-cell example and the split in Lemma C\(_W\). The fixes:

  • the calibration family needs \(\theta>p-2\);
  • block sums are exempted, not merely uncharged, and the entry now names why exemption is no longer blocked;
  • the degree remark is a necessary condition, and realizability is conditional on free cells;
  • the row-sum remark was wrong, since row sums over complementary sets are opposite modulo \(W\) and imposing all row equations with \(O\) is inconsistent, so it is now an open question;
  • the unused two-neighbour hypothesis now carries the local consistency of the empty system;
  • four points of wording.

These fixes remove or weaken claims, and the root statement is elementary, so no second pass was run. No computation was run.
